Lead-based paint debris from residences is excluded household waste under federal rules and may go to C&D or municipal landfills. Lead debris from non-residential work may be hazardous waste if it fails the TCLP test. States can be stricter.
facts.note: EPA's July 2000 interpretation and June 2003 rule allow residential lead-based paint waste from contractors to be disposed of as household waste.
facts.reviewed: Overstated. EPA treats residential lead-based paint debris from renovation as excluded household waste (2000 interpretation and 2003 rule), so it can go to C&D or municipal landfills. Non-residential lead debris is hazardous only if it fails TCLP

facts.fact: EPA's lead pre-renovation education and RRP rules apply in pre-1978 housing and child-occupied facilities when renovation disturbs more than 6 sq ft of painted surface per room inside or more than 20 sq ft outside, or involves window replacement or demolition of painted surfaces.
facts.note: Card says compliance is required when 2 sq ft or more is disturbed. The 2 sq ft minor-repair threshold came from the original 1998 rule; the 2008 RRP rule raised it to 6 sq ft interior per room and 20 sq ft exterior.

facts.fact: Before renovating pre-1978 housing, the renovator must give the owner and occupants EPA's Renovate Right lead pamphlet and get written acknowledgment. RRP records, including proof of pamphlet delivery, must be kept for 3 years after the renovation is completed.

facts.source: EPA 40 CFR 745.84 (Renovation, Repair and Painting Rule)
facts.fact: Before a paid renovation of a pre-1978 home or child-occupied facility, the renovation firm must give the owner and occupants EPA's 'Renovate Right' lead pamphlet no more than 60 days before work starts and get a signed acknowledgment (or proof of mailing).

facts.source: TSCA section 16; EPA civil monetary penalty inflation adjustment rule (40 CFR 19.4)
facts.fact: Violations of EPA lead-based paint rules (such as the RRP Rule) carry civil penalties per violation per day that are adjusted for inflation every year; the cap is now well above the old $37,500 figure (it passed $48,000 per violation per day in the 2024 adjustment).
facts.note: Card says up to $37,500 per day. That was the cap before the 2015 inflation-adjustment law; EPA now raises the TSCA maximum every year (about $48,512 in 2024 and roughly $49,772 in 2025). Check the current year's figure in 40 CFR 19.4.

facts.fact: Lead abatement means work designed to permanently eliminate lead-based paint hazards (for example removal, enclosure or encapsulation meant to last). It is regulated separately from ordinary renovation, which disturbs paint but is not aimed at permanent hazard removal.

facts.source: National Environmental Policy Act, 42 USC 4321 et seq.
facts.fact: NEPA applies to major federal actions, such as projects that are federally funded, federally permitted or on federal land, and requires their environmental effects to be evaluated.

Before any demolition or renovation, the affected part of the building must be thoroughly inspected for asbestos. Many states, and EPA guidance, require or expect an accredited asbestos inspector. The regulating agency must be notified at least 10 working days before demolition, or before a renovation above the regulated asbestos thresholds, begins.
facts.reviewed: 40 CFR 61.145 requires a thorough inspection but does not itself require an accredited inspector. Accreditation comes from AHERA/MAP and state rules

facts.source: TSCA Section 16; 40 CFR Part 19 (civil penalty inflation adjustments)
facts.fact: Violating EPA lead-based paint rules (such as the RRP rule) can bring civil penalties per violation per day. The cap started at $37,500 and is adjusted every year for inflation; it was above $48,000 by the 2024 adjustment. Check 40 CFR 19.4 for the current maximum.
facts.note: Card says up to $37,500 per day, the original 2008-era amount. EPA adjusts TSCA penalties annually for inflation and the current maximum is well above that.
facts.reviewed: Stated a 'current' penalty level; the figure is indexed every year, so it now carries a date

facts.fact: Lead abatement means measures designed to permanently eliminate lead-based paint hazards, unlike interim controls, which reduce hazards temporarily.

facts.source: Clean Water Act NPDES; EPA Construction General Permit
facts.fact: A federal NPDES stormwater permit is required for construction that disturbs 1 acre or more, or less than 1 acre if part of a larger common plan of development that disturbs 1 acre or more.
A brownfield is real property whose expansion, redevelopment or reuse may be complicated by the presence or potential presence of a hazardous substance, pollutant or contaminant.

A bid package typically includes the invitation to bid, instructions to bidders, the bid form, drawings and specifications, and any supplements or addenda. An addendum is a change to the bidding documents issued before bids are due (and before the owner-contractor agreement is signed); change orders are not part of a bid because they modify a contract after it is executed.

facts.source: Construction bidding ethics; Sherman Antitrust Act, 15 U.S.C. 1
facts.fact: Bid shopping is a contractor using one subcontractor's price to pressure other subs (including ones who never bid) into undercutting it, an unethical practice. Bid rigging is collusion among competitors to fix who wins a contract and is a federal crime under antitrust law.
The card set claims a good detailed estimate should fall within 1% to 2% of the actual construction cost.
facts.note: This accuracy target appears to come from the study guide; accuracy expectations vary by estimate type and are not a fixed industry standard.

facts.fact: A site visit is one of the most important steps in estimating because access, soil, existing conditions and logistics affect cost. An estimator who ignores company resources, location and risk puts the company's profitability at risk.

The quantity take-off method is a detailed estimating method in which the estimator measures and prices each unit of material and labor for every task; subcontractor quotes are carried separately rather than on the task material list. Tasks are grouped by type of activity (commonly CSI MasterFormat divisions) for ease of estimating.

Labor costs are estimated using the company's historical job-cost data and published productivity guides, combined with industry knowledge; crew size, worker skill level and weather all affect labor productivity and therefore labor cost.

Labor burden is the employer's cost on top of base wages: employer payroll taxes (Social Security, Medicare, FUTA, SUTA), workers' compensation and liability insurance premiums, and fringe benefits. Regular pay itself is not labor burden.

Equipment needed for a job, including special tools, is a direct cost carried in the equipment estimate. Rented equipment is priced at the rental (and operator, if supplied) hourly rate plus operating costs such as fuel, maintenance and delivery; equipment needs can also be met by leasing.

Project (job) overhead covers job-related costs that are not labor or materials, such as bonds, permits, temporary office and storage trailers, temporary utilities, dumpsters, portable toilets and site security. Company (general) overhead is the cost of running the business whether or not a job is underway, such as office rent, accounting and legal fees, office phones and administrative salaries.
The card set states that project overhead typically accounts for about 5% to 10% of the total bid.
facts.note: Rule-of-thumb percentage from the study guide; actual job overhead varies widely by project type and size.

facts.fact: Markup must cover overhead and profit: if it is too low the contractor may fail to recover its costs, and if it is too high the bid will not be competitive and will not win work.

A conceptual estimate is an early, order-of-magnitude estimate usually prepared by the architect using cost models from previous projects. The square-foot method multiplies the project's floor area by a cost per square foot, and the unit-price method bundles material, labor and equipment into a single price per unit of work.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: labor burden
facts.fact: A contractor's true labor cost includes the labor burden on top of wages: workers' compensation insurance, the employer's share of Social Security and Medicare, federal and state unemployment taxes, and any benefits.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: job costing and overhead
facts.fact: Direct costs can be charged to one project, such as job materials, field labor and subcontractor costs. Indirect costs (overhead) cannot be traced to one job and are spread across many; examples are office rent and a year-end bonus not tied to a particular project.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: purchasing and job costing
facts.fact: Purchase orders record exactly what was ordered, the price and the terms, which helps control and organize expenses. A material's total cost includes its price plus shipping and delivery charges.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: labor burden
facts.fact: True labor cost includes more than wages: the employer's payroll taxes (FICA, FUTA, SUTA), workers' compensation insurance and fringe benefits are part of the labor burden.
A bid alternate is a price, requested in the bid documents, for using a different material, product or scope than the base bid, so the owner can decide which options to accept.
Material quantities for a bid are measured (taken off) from the construction drawings, with the specifications defining the required quality and type of each material.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: estimating (general conditions)
facts.fact: General conditions costs such as supervision, the field office, and temporary utilities depend on time and are usually spread evenly across the project duration.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: estimating methods
facts.fact: Estimating methods range from conceptual (cost per square foot or per unit from past projects) to detailed quantity take-off. The square-foot method multiplies building area by a unit cost per square foot, while take-off prices each material and labor item one by one and is the most accurate.

facts.source: CSI MasterFormat; NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: estimating
facts.fact: Estimates are easier to build and check when quantities and tasks are grouped by type of work, commonly following CSI MasterFormat divisions.
A bid is a contractor's signed proposal offering to perform defined work for a stated price; it becomes binding once accepted under the terms of the solicitation.

A job cost system tracks actual costs against the estimate for each project, which lets the contractor monitor costs during the job, report results, base future labor-hour estimates on past performance, and make strategic decisions; using standard estimating formats and forms also reduces errors.
Working capital equals current assets minus current liabilities. Tracking cash coming in and going out during a project helps ensure the contractor has enough working capital to finish the job.
facts.note: Card defines working capital as 'cash available after liabilities or debts are paid'. The accounting definition is current assets minus current liabilities, which includes receivables and inventory, not just cash.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: job cost accounting
facts.fact: The simplest way to track a project budget is a job cost system that compares actual costs, by cost code, against the original cost estimate.
Bookkeeping is recording a business's financial transactions in a systematic way. Managers base financial decisions on those records.
The general ledger holds every account of the business (assets, liabilities, equity, revenue, expenses). Its account balances are used to prepare the financial statements.

Noncash entries such as depreciation, accruals, adjusting entries and corrections go in the general journal. The special journals (cash receipts, cash disbursements, payroll) handle routine cash transactions.

A source document is created whenever money is paid or received, a debt is incurred or a receivable arises, and it proves the transaction happened. Examples are receipts, customer and vendor invoices, purchase orders, deposit slips and time cards. Cash itself is not a source document.
The three basic financial statements are the balance sheet, the income statement (profit and loss statement) and the statement of cash flows.

An asset is anything of value the business owns. Current assets are cash and items expected to turn into cash within one year (such as receivables). Fixed assets are long-lived items used in the business, such as land, buildings, equipment and furniture; an office building, for example, is fixed, not current.

A liability is any debt or obligation the business owes. Current liabilities are due within one year, such as a six-month note or the part of a long-term equipment loan due in the next 12 months. Long-term liabilities are due more than one year out.
The balance sheet follows the accounting equation: Assets = Liabilities + Owner's Equity. It shows the company's financial position at one specific date.

Owner's equity is the owners' stake in the business: their initial and later investments plus retained earnings. The balance sheet does not show the owner's personal finances, the market value of the business, or cash flows (those go on the cash flow statement).

The income statement (profit and loss statement) shows revenue and expenses over a period, so it reflects the company's operations. It does not show the cash balance. Gross profit = revenue minus cost of goods sold (direct job costs). Net income (net profit) = revenue minus all expenses.

Liquidity ratios measure whether a company can pay the obligations coming due in the next year. Current ratio = current assets ÷ current liabilities. Quick (acid-test) ratio = (current assets − inventory) ÷ current liabilities; for example, ($60,000 − $15,000) ÷ $40,000 = 1.125.
Activity (efficiency) ratios measure how well a company uses its assets and manages credit. Examples are receivables turnover and the average collection period.
Debt ratio = total debt ÷ total assets. For example, $56,655 of debt ÷ $75,387 of assets ≈ 0.75, meaning creditors fund about 75% of the assets.
The profitability ratio (net profit margin) = net income after taxes ÷ revenue. Return on total assets = net profit after taxes ÷ total assets.

Under the cash method, income is reported when it is received and expenses are deducted when they are paid. Its main weakness is that revenue and the expenses that produced it often fall in different periods, which distorts the company's true financial picture.
Under the accrual method, income is recorded when it is earned, even if not yet collected, and expenses are recorded when incurred, even if not yet paid. This matches revenue with the related costs.

A contractor may use the completed-contract method on a construction contract it expects to finish within 2 years if its average annual gross receipts for the 3 prior tax years are under the IRC 448(c) limit. That limit is $25 million indexed for inflation ($31 million for tax years beginning in 2025). Home construction contracts are exempt from percentage-of-completion regardless of size.
facts.note: Card says $10 million. That was the limit before the 2017 Tax Cuts and Jobs Act, which raised it to $25 million indexed for inflation starting in 2018 ($30M for 2024, $31M for 2025). Check the current year's indexed amount.

facts.fact: The completed-contract method's main advantage is tax deferral: no income from the contract is reported until it is finished. A 'long-term contract' for tax purposes is a building or construction contract that is not finished in the tax year it was entered into, so the method you may use depends on contract type, average gross receipts and whether the contract is finished at year end.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: equipment management
facts.fact: A contractor should keep a separate record for each piece of equipment, including purchase cost, maintenance and repair costs, fuel and depreciation. These records let equipment costs be charged accurately to jobs.
Depreciation spreads an asset's cost over its useful life. Straight-line depreciation per year = (cost − salvage value) ÷ useful life in years, so the same amount is written off each year.

Accelerated depreciation writes off more of the asset's cost in its early years, which gives larger early tax deductions; it suits assets likely to be replaced early. Declining-balance and MACRS calculations apply a set rate or table without first subtracting salvage value (MACRS treats salvage as zero).

'2/10 net 30' means a 2% discount if paid within 10 days, otherwise the full amount is due in 30 days; a $1,000 invoice paid within 10 days costs $980. '1/10 net 30' gives a 1% discount for payment within 10 days.
Fixed assets are long-term tangible assets used to run the business, such as equipment, vehicles, buildings and land, and they are depreciated (except land).
Owner's equity is the owner's stake in the business: what the owner invested plus retained earnings, equal to total assets minus total liabilities.
Gross profit equals revenue minus cost of goods sold (for a contractor, direct construction costs); net profit then subtracts overhead and other expenses.
Net income divided by revenue is the net profit margin, a profitability ratio showing how much of each sales dollar is kept as profit.
The main drawback of cash-basis accounting is that revenue and expenses are recorded when cash moves, so expenses may not be matched to the revenue they produced in the same period.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: financial management
facts.fact: Front-end loading means placing extra value on early activities in the schedule of values so the contractor collects more in early pay applications, offsetting the cash-flow drag of the retainage the owner withholds.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: job cost accounting
facts.fact: Cost codes classify project costs by work item so that actual costs can be compared with the estimate and budget, which shows overruns early and improves future estimates.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: financial management
facts.fact: A project budget is built from the accepted estimate, which becomes the baseline for tracking job costs.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: cash flow / financial management
facts.fact: A cumulative cash flow (S) curve that rises steeply at the start shows a front-loaded project, where much of the cost or billing falls early; cash flow projections are built by tying the schedule of values to the construction schedule.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: job cost accounting
facts.fact: Job cost documentation has two main purposes: to feed cost data into the company's accounting system and to build up information that lets managers control each project's costs.

Under the cash method, revenue is recorded when it is received and expenses when they are paid. Under the accrual method, revenue is recorded when earned and expenses when incurred, regardless of when the cash actually moves.
facts.reviewed: 'whenever the cash actually moves' reads as the opposite of accrual accounting; it should say 'regardless of when'

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: equipment cost accounting
facts.fact: A separate record for each piece of equipment should track its costs, such as purchase cost, depreciation, maintenance and repair, fuel and operating hours, so equipment rates can be charged to jobs and replacement decisions made.

facts.source: 29 CFR 570.35 (FLSA child labor, hours for 14 and 15 year olds)
facts.fact: Under the FLSA, 14- and 15-year-olds may work only between 7 a.m. and 7 p.m. (until 9 p.m. from June 1 through Labor Day), with daily and weekly hour limits during school periods.
facts.note: Card says a 15-year-old may not begin work before 6 a.m.; 29 CFR 570.35 sets the earliest start at 7 a.m.

facts.fact: Minors can work for a construction company, but 14- and 15-year-olds are barred from construction work except office or sales jobs away from the site, and 16- and 17-year-olds may not do jobs covered by the hazardous occupations orders, including roofing, wrecking and demolition, trenching and excavation, and running most power-driven woodworking machines.
Georgia requires an employment certificate (work permit) for minors under 18 who have not graduated from high school or earned a GED.
facts.note: State-specific rule from the card; not confirmed against the current Georgia statute.

facts.fact: Form I-9 verifies the identity and employment authorization of every person hired in the U.S., citizens and noncitizens alike. It is required by the Immigration and Nationality Act as amended by IRCA and applies to all employers regardless of size.
facts.note: Card says the I-9 shows legal immigration status. It verifies identity and authorization to work, and U.S. citizens complete it too. Card also says the INA applies to employers of '1 or more'; the I-9 requirement applies to every employer regardless of size.

facts.fact: A new employee must complete Section 1 of Form I-9 no later than the first day of work, and the employer must examine documents and complete Section 2 within 3 business days after the employee's first day.
Employers must keep each Form I-9 for 3 years after the date of hire or 1 year after employment ends, whichever is later.
facts.note: Card says '3 years and for 1 year after employee is terminated', which implies both periods. The rule is whichever of the two dates is later.

facts.source: USCIS Form I-9 Lists of Acceptable Documents
facts.fact: An unrestricted Social Security card is a List C document: it proves employment authorization but not identity, so it must be paired with a List B identity document such as a driver's license. A bank statement is not an acceptable I-9 document.
The federal minimum wage is $7.25 per hour, but employers may pay employees under 20 years old a youth minimum wage of $4.25 per hour during their first 90 consecutive calendar days of employment.

The FLSA's main wage requirements are paying covered non-exempt employees at least the federal minimum wage and paying overtime of at least 1.5 times the regular rate for hours over 40 in a workweek. The FLSA also sets child labor and recordkeeping rules.

The FLSA has no minimum number of employees. It covers enterprises with at least two employees and at least $500,000 in annual business volume (plus hospitals, schools and government), and it also covers individual employees engaged in interstate commerce, so nearly all contractors are covered.
facts.note: Card says the FLSA applies to all employers with 1 or more employees. Coverage is based on enterprise dollar volume or individual interstate-commerce activity, not an employee-count threshold.

facts.fact: A meal break is unpaid only if the employee is completely relieved of duty. If a worker must answer phones during lunch, that time counts as hours worked even if he is clocked out, so 8 hours plus a 30-minute working lunch for 5 days is 42.5 hours, with 2.5 hours owed at time and a half.

Under the FLSA, a workweek is a fixed, regularly recurring period of 168 hours (seven consecutive 24-hour periods) that may begin on any day and hour. Each workweek stands alone: hours cannot be averaged across weeks, so a worker who works 37 hours one week and 43 the next is owed 3 overtime hours in the second week.

Non-exempt employees are those entitled to minimum wage and overtime; laborers, hourly carpenters and other manual or blue-collar workers are non-exempt no matter how much they earn. Overtime that the employer suffers or permits must be paid even if it was not authorized, although the employer may discipline the worker.

Exempt employees, such as bona fide executives, administrative and professional staff, are not owed overtime, but they must be paid on a salary basis above the DOL salary threshold and their actual duties must meet the exemption tests; job title alone does not make someone exempt.
The FLSA does not require employers to provide paid vacation, holidays, sick leave, severance or (for adults) rest or meal breaks; these are matters of company policy, contract or state law.

For each non-exempt worker, FLSA records must include identifying information, the day and hour the workweek begins, hours worked each workday and each workweek, pay rate, straight-time and overtime earnings, deductions and pay dates. No particular form or time clock is required.

Willful violations of the FLSA can be prosecuted criminally, with fines up to $10,000; a second conviction can also bring imprisonment of up to 6 months. Employers also face back wages, liquidated damages and civil money penalties.

The ADA's employment provisions (Title I) apply to employers with 15 or more employees. They prohibit discrimination against qualified individuals with disabilities and require reasonable accommodation.

facts.source: 29 CFR 1630.2 (ADA definitions, as amended by ADAAA)
facts.fact: People with HIV/AIDS are protected under the ADA. Temporary, short-term conditions such as a broken arm or the flu generally are not disabilities, although a temporary impairment that is severe enough can qualify under the ADA Amendments Act.

The FMLA gives eligible employees up to 12 workweeks of unpaid, job-protected leave in a 12-month period, with group health coverage kept in place, for the birth of a child, adoption or foster placement, caring for a spouse, child or parent with a serious health condition, or the employee's own serious health condition. It applies to private employers with 50 or more employees.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: employee handbooks
facts.fact: Company employee handbooks cover policies for current employees (pay, conduct, benefits, safety); hiring practices are generally kept out of the employee manual.
facts.note: From a multiple-choice card with no options shown; cannot confirm this is a firm rule.

facts.fact: Under the FLSA, work an employer suffers or permits is paid work time, so unauthorized overtime by a non-exempt employee must still be paid at the overtime rate; the employer may discipline the employee but cannot withhold the pay.

facts.source: Personal Responsibility and Work Opportunity Reconciliation Act of 1996; 42 USC 653a
facts.fact: Employers must report newly hired employees to their state's new-hire registry, and the data goes into the National Directory of New Hires, which is used mainly to locate parents and enforce child support orders.

A meal break counts as unpaid time only if the employee is fully relieved of duty. A non-exempt worker who must answer phones during a 30-minute clocked-out lunch is working, so in a week of five 8-hour days those 2.5 hours must be paid at 1.5 times the regular rate.

For non-exempt employees the FLSA requires records of hours worked each workday and each workweek, wages and pay data, but does not require any specific timekeeping method or a record of the clock time the employee left each day.

facts.source: Family and Medical Leave Act, 29 CFR 825.110 and 825.112
facts.fact: FMLA gives eligible employees up to 12 weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave in 12 months for birth of a child, adoption or foster placement, their own serious health condition, or caring for a spouse, child or parent with one. Eligibility requires 12 months of employment, 1,250 hours worked in the past 12 months, and 50 employees within 75 miles.

An employer owes federal unemployment (FUTA) tax if it paid wages of $1,500 or more in any calendar quarter, or had at least one employee for some part of a day in 20 or more different weeks, in the current or prior year. FUTA is paid only by the employer, and state unemployment tax is also employer-paid in most states (a few, such as Alaska, New Jersey and Pennsylvania, also withhold from employees).

Federal law requires employers to report each new hire or rehire to their state's new hire directory within 20 days of hire, or sooner if the state sets a shorter deadline. States forward the data to the National Directory of New Hires, which is used mainly to enforce child support orders.
A state may fine an employer for failing to report a new hire, capped by federal law at $25 per unreported employee, or $500 if the failure results from a conspiracy between employer and employee.
Georgia requires employers to report new hires and rehires to the Georgia New Hire Reporting Program within 10 days of the hire date.
facts.note: State-specific deadline; believed to be 10 days but should be confirmed against the current Georgia statute.

facts.fact: Employees complete IRS Form W-4 so the employer can calculate how much federal income tax to withhold from their pay.

An employer owes federal unemployment (FUTA) tax if it paid wages of $1,500 or more in any calendar quarter, or had at least one employee for some part of a day in 20 or more different weeks, in the current or prior year. FUTA is 6.0% on the first $7,000 of each employee's wages, usually reduced to 0.6% by the state credit.

facts.source: Georgia Department of Labor (state unemployment tax)
facts.fact: Georgia's state unemployment tax wage base has been $9,500 per employee per calendar year since 2013 (still $9,500 as of 2025). It is separate from the federal FUTA wage base of $7,000. Confirm the current Georgia figure with the Georgia Department of Labor.
facts.note: Cards say unemployment contributions are paid on the first $8,500. Georgia's taxable wage base has been $9,500 since 2013, and the federal FUTA base is $7,000. Re-check the Georgia figure each year.
facts.reviewed: Stated a state wage base that can change each year as if it were permanent; it now carries a date

facts.source: Georgia Department of Labor (new employer rate)
facts.fact: New employers in Georgia are assigned a standard beginning unemployment tax rate (the card gives 2.7%) until they have enough experience to receive an experience-based rate.
facts.note: Georgia's new-employer rate and add-on assessments change; 2.7% from the card was not confirmed for the current year.

facts.source: IRS Pub 15-A; IRS common-law rules (behavioral control, financial control, relationship of the parties)
facts.fact: The IRS decides worker status by looking at behavioral control, financial control and the relationship of the parties. A worker whose methods and finances the business does not control, who gets no employee benefits, and whose relationship is not permanent or ongoing is generally an independent contractor.

No single factor decides worker status. A verbal rather than written agreement, piece-rate pay, or supplying one's own tools does not by itself make someone an independent contractor, and full-time, continuing work that the business regularly inspects and directs points toward employee status.

facts.source: IRS Pub 15-T; Form W-4 (2020 and later)
facts.fact: Employers figure federal income tax withholding from the employee's Form W-4 (filing status, dependents and other adjustments) using the methods and tables in IRS Pub 15-T.
facts.note: Card says withholding follows the tax table and 'number of exemptions'. Since the 2020 redesign of Form W-4, withholding allowances and exemptions are no longer used, and personal exemptions were suspended by the 2017 tax law. Withholding tables moved from Pub 15 to Pub 15-T.

facts.fact: An employee who claims exemption from federal income tax withholding must give the employer a new Form W-4 by February 15 each year to keep the exemption.

Social Security tax is 6.2% on wages up to the annual wage base ($176,100 for 2025), and Medicare tax is 1.45% on all wages. Employee and employer each pay these rates. Employees also pay an Additional Medicare Tax of 0.9% on wages over $200,000, with no employer match.
Employers must withhold federal income tax and the employee's share of FICA (Social Security and Medicare) from paychecks. FUTA is paid only by the employer and is never withheld from wages.
C corporations file their federal income tax return on Form 1120, and S corporations file Form 1120-S.

A sole proprietor with no withholding on business profits avoids the underpayment penalty by making quarterly estimated tax payments (Form 1040-ES), due about April 15, June 15, September 15 and January 15.

All federal employment tax deposits must be made by electronic funds transfer, usually through EFTPS. A small liability (under $2,500 for the quarter) may instead be paid with a timely filed Form 941.
facts.note: Card says payroll taxes can be mailed with a payment coupon. Paper deposit coupons (Form 8109) were discontinued January 1, 2011, and deposits must now be made electronically.

facts.fact: Employers must keep employment tax records for at least 4 years after the tax is due or paid, whichever is later.
IRS Publication 15, Circular E (the Employer's Tax Guide), explains employer duties to withhold, deposit, report and pay employment taxes. The withholding tables are now in companion Pub 15-T.

An employer is a monthly depositor for Form 941 taxes if its total liability in the lookback period (the four quarters ending June 30 of the prior year) was $50,000 or less, and a semiweekly depositor if it was more than $50,000. Any day's accumulated liability of $100,000 or more must be deposited the next business day.

facts.source: IRS General Instructions for Forms W-2 and W-3
facts.fact: Employers report each employee's annual wages and withholding on Form W-2. They must give W-2s to employees and file them with the Social Security Administration by January 31.

Form 941, the Employer's Quarterly Federal Tax Return, reports wages paid and the federal income tax, Social Security and Medicare tax withheld each quarter. Most employers file it every quarter (exceptions: small employers the IRS notifies to file annual Form 944, agricultural employers who use Form 943, and household employers). If the quarter's total liability is under $2,500, the tax may be paid with the return; otherwise it must be deposited on the monthly or semiweekly schedule.
facts.note: Card suggests Form 941 is used only when reporting under $2,500 for the quarter. In fact most employers file 941 quarterly; the $2,500 test decides only whether the tax may be paid with the return instead of deposited.
facts.reviewed: Not every employer files Form 941. Employers told to file Form 944, agricultural employers (Form 943) and household employers (Schedule H) do not

facts.fact: The IRS failure-to-deposit penalty is 2% if the deposit is 1-5 days late, 5% if 6-15 days late, and 10% if more than 15 days late (or not made electronically). It rises to 15% if the tax is still unpaid more than 10 days after the first IRS notice. The same tiers apply to FUTA deposits, so a FUTA deposit 7 days late draws 5%.
facts.note: Cards say the 10% penalty applies to deposits more than 16 days late and that penalties run '2% up to 10%'. The 10% tier starts at more than 15 days, and a 15% tier applies after an IRS notice goes unanswered.

facts.source: IRC 6041A; Form 1099-NEC instructions; One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025) section 70433
facts.fact: Payments for services to an unincorporated independent contractor (such as a sole-proprietor HVAC sub) are reported on Form 1099-NEC. The threshold was $600 or more per year for payments through 2025 and is $2,000 for payments made in 2026 and later, indexed for inflation after that. Payments to corporations generally need no 1099.
facts.note: Cards say amounts over $600 paid to contractors are 'wages' reported on 'Form 1099'. Nonemployee pay is not wages; since tax year 2020 it goes on Form 1099-NEC, not 1099-MISC. The 2025 tax law raised the threshold from $600 to $2,000 for payments after December 31, 2025. Verify the threshold for the year in question.

facts.fact: FUTA is 6.0% of the first $7,000 of each employee's annual wages. Employers that pay state unemployment tax on time get a credit of up to 5.4%, so the net rate is usually 0.6% (higher in credit-reduction states).
facts.note: Card only says FUTA is figured 'at the current prevailing rate according to the IRS'. The actual rule is 6.0% on the first $7,000 of wages, with up to a 5.4% state credit (net 0.6%).

facts.fact: FUTA tax must be deposited quarterly once the accumulated liability exceeds $500, by the last day of the month after the quarter ends. The annual Form 940 is due January 31, or February 10 if all FUTA deposits were made on time.
facts.note: Card says that owing over $500 means you must 'file' quarterly. What is quarterly is the deposit; Form 940 is filed once a year by January 31.

facts.source: Georgia Department of Revenue withholding payment schedules
facts.fact: Georgia sets each employer's state withholding payment schedule from a lookback period (July 1 through June 30 of the prior year). Employers whose liability is under the state threshold (reported as $50,000) pay monthly.
facts.note: State-specific, and the card is vague. Georgia uses a lookback period and monthly/semiweekly schedules similar to the federal rules, but confirm current thresholds (including any quarterly filer tier) with Georgia DOR.

facts.fact: Georgia's corporate income tax rate is no longer 6%. It dropped to 5.75% in 2019 and has since been cut further alongside the individual rate (5.39% for 2024 and 5.19% for 2025), with more step-downs scheduled.
facts.note: Card says 6%, the rate before 2019. Because the rate now changes year to year by legislation, confirm the current-year rate with Georgia DOR before relying on an exact figure.

facts.fact: Medicare tax is 1.45% of all wages for the employee and another 1.45% for the employer, and the employer must withhold an extra 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax on an employee's wages above $200,000 in a year (employee only). Social Security tax is 6.2% each, up to the annual wage base.
A profitable sole proprietor has no employer withholding on business income, so they avoid the underpayment penalty by making quarterly estimated tax payments (Form 1040-ES).

Federal payroll tax deposits must be made by electronic funds transfer, usually through EFTPS; paper deposit coupons (Form 8109) were discontinued after 2010. An employer with less than $2,500 of liability for the quarter may instead pay with a timely filed Form 941.
facts.note: Card says corporations may mail deposits with a payment coupon. The IRS eliminated Form 8109 deposit coupons as of January 1, 2011; deposits must be made electronically.

facts.fact: An employer whose total employment taxes in the lookback period were $50,000 or less deposits monthly; more than $50,000 means semiweekly deposits, and a $100,000 liability on any day must be deposited the next business day.
Failure-to-deposit penalties: 2% for deposits 1-5 days late, 5% for 6-15 days late, 10% for more than 15 days late, and 15% if still unpaid 10 days after the first IRS notice.
If accumulated FUTA tax exceeds $500 at the end of a quarter, it must be deposited by the last day of the month after that quarter; the Form 940 return itself is filed once a year, due January 31.
facts.note: Card says unemployment tax over $500 must be filed quarterly. The deposit is quarterly; the FUTA return (Form 940) is filed annually.

facts.source: IRS General Instructions for Information Returns (1099-NEC, 1099-MISC)
facts.fact: Recipient copies of Form 1099-NEC (used since tax year 2020 for nonemployee compensation paid to subcontractors) and most Form 1099-MISC must be furnished by January 31.

The small-contractor exception that allows the completed-contract method (instead of percentage of completion) applies to contracts expected to finish within 2 years by contractors whose average annual gross receipts for the prior 3 years do not exceed the inflation-indexed limit ($25 million base; $31 million for tax years beginning in 2025).
facts.note: Card says $10 million, the pre-2018 limit. The Tax Cuts and Jobs Act raised it to $25 million indexed for inflation.

facts.fact: Payments for services to an independent contractor who is a sole proprietor (not an employee) are reported on Form 1099-NEC; payments to corporations are generally exempt.

Social Security tax is 6.2% of wages from the employee plus a matching 6.2% from the employer, up to the annual wage base. Medicare is 1.45% each with no wage cap, plus an extra 0.9% withheld from an employee's wages over $200,000.
Float (slack) is the amount of time an activity can be delayed in starting or finishing without delaying the project completion date. Activities on the critical path have zero float.

The three common scheduling methods are calendar scheduling, bar charts (Gantt charts) and the critical path method. Calendar scheduling ties tasks to specific dates and can be done on a simple calendar; a bar chart shows each activity's duration and sequence but not how activities depend on each other.

The critical path method (CPM) shows the logical relationships between activities; the longest chain of dependent activities (the critical path) sets the minimum overall project duration, so any delay to a critical activity delays the whole project. CPM is regarded as the best method for scheduling construction.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: project management roles
facts.fact: The project manager is responsible for the job budget, schedule, cost control and overall management of the project, while bidding is normally handled by the estimator. The superintendent oversees daily on-site operations and typically drives completion of the punch list.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: project management roles
facts.fact: The foreman assists the superintendent with daily operations, directs the crew and is often responsible for training employees in the field.
facts.note: Division of duties among superintendent and foreman varies by company; training assignment to the foreman matches the card and NASCLA convention but is not a universal rule.

facts.fact: On projects using AIA documents, the architect (sometimes an engineer) reviews the contractor's application for payment and certifies the amount due before the owner makes a progress payment.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: job documentation
facts.fact: A daily log (job diary) records facts that affect progress, such as weather, workers and hours on site, equipment, deliveries, visitors, work completed and delays. It is key evidence for time-extension claims such as rain delays and should stay factual, without personal comments or opinions.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: materials management
facts.fact: Just-in-time delivery, ordering materials by construction phase so they arrive close to when they will be installed, keeps job-site inventory low, which reduces storage space needed and losses from theft and damage.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: value engineering
facts.fact: Value engineering is a systematic review of a project's design, materials and methods to deliver the required function and the owner's cost, quality and time priorities at the lowest life-cycle cost without reducing performance.
Shop drawings are prepared by subcontractors or suppliers; the contractor must review and approve them first, then submit them to the architect for review against the design intent.

The contractor is responsible for assembling closeout requirements such as warranties, O&M manuals, lien releases and record documents, while the architect inspects and certifies substantial and final completion for the owner.
facts.note: Card says the project architect is responsible to the contractor for meeting all closeout and filing requirements. Under standard AIA documents the contractor gathers closeout items and the architect reviews and certifies completion on the owner's behalf.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: project delivery methods
facts.fact: In agency construction management, the owner holds separate contracts with the designer, the contractor(s), and a construction manager who acts only as the owner's advisor and does not guarantee cost.
Final as-built records should include, along with marked-up as-built drawings, photographs of conditions, especially concealed work such as underground and in-wall utilities taken before cover-up.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: project documentation
facts.fact: Daily logs (job diaries) record weather, crews, work done and delays each day, and are the main evidence supporting a claim for a time extension such as for rain days.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: materials management
facts.fact: Just-in-time delivery schedules materials to arrive shortly before they are installed, which reduces the storage space needed on site and the risk of theft or damage.
Float (slack) is how long an activity can be delayed past its early start or finish without delaying the project completion date; critical-path activities have zero float.
A bar (Gantt) chart shows activity durations on a timeline, while a CPM schedule also shows the logical dependencies between activities, which lets it identify the critical path and float.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: project delivery methods
facts.fact: In design-build, the owner signs one contract with a single entity that is responsible for both design and construction and assembles the team of architects, engineers and builders.

facts.source: Construction risk management practice (certificates of insurance)
facts.fact: Before hiring a subcontractor, a contractor should verify the sub's insurance coverage (general liability and workers' compensation) by obtaining a current certificate of insurance; an uninsured sub's workers may otherwise become the hiring contractor's liability.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: safety programs
facts.fact: Accidents caused by unsafe conditions cost a contractor productivity and profit. A safety and health program reduces injuries and workers' compensation premiums and improves productivity, morale and profitability.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: risk management
facts.fact: Before a subcontractor starts work, the prime contractor should get and check certificates of insurance (general liability and workers' compensation) for that sub. If the sub is uninsured, injury claims and insurance premium-audit charges can fall back on the prime.

Employers with more than 10 employees at any time in the previous calendar year must keep OSHA injury and illness records (construction is not a partially exempt industry). A construction operation expected to last one year or more is a separate establishment needing its own OSHA 300 log; shorter projects may be recorded on one log.

OSHA Form 300 is the Log of Work-Related Injuries and Illnesses, listing each recordable case; Form 300A is the annual summary, posted from February 1 to April 30; Form 301 is the Injury and Illness Incident Report, completed within 7 calendar days of learning of the case.
Employers must keep OSHA Forms 300, 300A and 301 for 5 years following the end of the calendar year the records cover.
Employee exposure records must be kept for at least 30 years, and employee medical records for the duration of employment plus 30 years.
An employer must report a work-related fatality to OSHA within 8 hours, and any in-patient hospitalization of one or more employees, an amputation or loss of an eye within 24 hours.
facts.note: Card says the fatality or hospitalization of 3 or more employees must be reported within 8 hours. That was the pre-2015 rule; since January 1, 2015, a single hospitalization, amputation or eye loss must be reported within 24 hours and any fatality within 8 hours.

facts.fact: OSHA civil penalties are maximums adjusted for inflation each January, not fixed or mandatory amounts. After the January 2025 adjustment, the maximum was $16,550 per serious or other-than-serious violation, including posting violations, and $165,514 per willful or repeated violation, with a willful minimum of $11,823.
facts.note: Cards give $7,000 as a 'mandatory' serious and posting penalty and $70,000 as the willful maximum. Those were the pre-2016 statutory caps; penalties have been inflation-adjusted every year since 2016 and are maximums the agency may reduce.

facts.fact: Knowingly making a false statement or falsifying records required under the OSH Act is a criminal offense punishable by a fine of up to $10,000, imprisonment of up to 6 months, or both.

OSHA inspections are either programmed (planned, such as targeting high-hazard industries or establishments with high injury rates) or unprogrammed (triggered by imminent danger, fatalities or catastrophes, complaints, referrals or follow-ups).

Programmed OSHA inspections are planned inspections aimed at high-hazard industries or establishments with high injury and illness rates; unprogrammed inspections respond to imminent danger, fatalities, complaints and referrals.
The OSHA 300 log, the 300A annual summary and the 301 incident reports must be kept for 5 years after the end of the calendar year they cover, with the 300 log updated during that period.

A prime contractor that contracts for full performance of a job takes on all employer obligations under OSHA's construction standards for the whole project, including work it subcontracts. Each subcontractor is also responsible for compliance on its own portion, so the responsibility is shared.

OSHA 1926.105 still requires safety nets where work is more than 25 ft above the ground, water or another surface and ladders, scaffolds, catch platforms, temporary floors, safety lines or safety belts are impractical. Separately, Subpart M requires guardrails, nets or personal fall arrest at 6 ft for most construction work, so 25 ft is not the general fall protection trigger.

OSHA construction Subpart E, Personal Protective and Life Saving Equipment, covers general PPE criteria, foot, head, hearing, eye and face, and respiratory protection, safety belts, lifelines and lanyards, safety nets, and working over or near water.

Wire rope used for rigging must be taken out of service if, in any length of eight rope diameters, the visible broken wires exceed 10 percent of the total number of wires, or if the rope shows other signs of excessive wear, corrosion or defects.

Hand-held powered circular saws, chain saws, and percussion tools without a positive accessory holding means must have a constant-pressure switch that cuts the power as soon as the operator releases it.
The limit of less than 30 psi for compressed air used in cleaning (with chip guarding and PPE) does not apply when cleaning concrete forms, mill scale or for similar purposes.
Workers using abrasive wheels must wear eye protection that meets Subpart E, unless eye shields permanently attached to the bench or floor stand give them adequate protection.
Bars may never be used under cylinder valves or valve protection caps to pry frozen compressed gas cylinders loose. Frozen cylinders are thawed with warm water, never boiling water.
Compressed gas cylinders must be secured upright at all times, except when necessary for short periods while they are actually being hoisted or carried.

Inside buildings, gas cylinders must be stored in a well-protected, well-ventilated, dry location at least 20 ft from highly combustible materials such as oil or excelsior. Their assigned places must be away from elevators, stairs and gangways, and never in unventilated enclosures such as lockers or cupboards.
facts.note: Card says at least 2 ft (6.1 m). 6.1 m is 20 ft. 1926.350(a)(11) requires 20 ft from highly combustible materials.

facts.fact: Before a regulator is connected, the cylinder valve is cracked (opened slightly and closed right away) to blow out dust and dirt. The worker stands to one side of the outlet, and a fuel-gas valve is never cracked where the gas could reach welding, sparks, flame or another ignition source.
When an arc welder or cutter leaves the work or stops for any appreciable time, or when the welding machine is going to be moved, the power supply switch to the equipment must be opened (turned off).

For electrical equipment at 151 to 600 volts to ground, the minimum clear working space in front is 3 ft when there are exposed live parts on one side and nothing live or grounded opposite. It is 3-1/2 ft when grounded parts (including concrete, brick or tile walls) are opposite, and 4 ft when there are exposed live parts on both sides.

Above 600 volts, OSHA's minimum depth of clear working space increases with voltage and exposure condition. For example, it is 3, 4 or 5 ft at 601 to 2,500 volts and 8, 10 or 12 ft above 75 kV, depending on whether the opposite side has no live or grounded parts, grounded parts, or exposed live parts.
An outrigger scaffold platform may be no more than 3 in from the face of the work. The general limit for other scaffolds is 14 in, or 18 in for plastering and lathing.

Unless it is cleated or otherwise restrained, each end of a scaffold platform must extend at least 6 in past the centerline of its support. A platform 10 ft or shorter may overhang its support by no more than 12 in, and a longer one by no more than 18 in, unless the overhang is designed to carry the load without tipping or is blocked off by guardrails.

Where scaffold platforms are overlapped to make a longer platform, the overlap must fall only over supports and be at least 12 in, unless the platforms are nailed together or otherwise kept from moving.

Scaffold components made by different manufacturers may be mixed only if they fit together without force and the scaffold's structural integrity is maintained. They may not be modified to make them fit unless a competent person determines that the result is structurally sound.

Legs, posts and frames of supported scaffolds must bear on base plates and mud sills or another firm foundation with level footings, and unstable objects may not be used as supports. Front-end loaders may hold platforms only if the manufacturer designed them for it, and forklifts only if the whole platform is attached to the forks and the forklift does not move horizontally while the platform is occupied.
facts.note: Card says forklifts shall not be used at all. 1926.451(c)(2)(v) permits a forklift to support a scaffold platform if the entire platform is attached to the fork and the forklift is not moved horizontally while the platform is occupied.

facts.fact: Workers on a scaffold more than 10 ft above a lower level must be protected from falling. On boatswains' chairs and on catenary, float, needle beam and ladder jack scaffolds the protection must be personal fall arrest, while most supported scaffolds may use either guardrails or personal fall arrest.

On scaffolds over 10 ft high, a worker on a crawling board (chicken ladder) must be protected by personal fall arrest, a guardrail, or a 3/4 in diameter grabline or equivalent handhold fastened beside the board. A walkway inside a scaffold needs a guardrail within 9-1/2 in of it along at least one side, and overhand bricklayers on supported scaffolds need guardrails or personal fall arrest on all open sides and ends except the side next to the wall being laid.
facts.reviewed: Omitted personal fall arrest as an option for crawling boards (1926.451(g)(1)(iii)); bricklayer rule covers open sides and ends

facts.fact: Toprails on supported scaffolds made or placed in service after January 1, 2000 must be 38 to 45 in above the platform. Older supported scaffolds, and suspended scaffolds that need both guardrails and fall arrest, may have toprails 36 to 45 in high.
Casters and wheels on mobile scaffolds must be locked with positive wheel and/or swivel locks, or an equivalent means, so the scaffold cannot move while it is used in one place.

Workers at wall openings, including openings with chutes attached, need guardrails, safety nets or personal fall arrest when the outside bottom edge of the opening is 6 ft or more above the lower level and the inside bottom edge is less than 39 in above the walking/working surface.

Balusters or other intermediate guardrail members between posts may be no more than 19 in apart. Other members, such as extra midrails or panels, must leave no opening in the guardrail system wider than 19 in.
facts.reviewed: Baluster spacing is in (b)(2)(iii); (b)(2)(iv) covers other members

facts.fact: Guardrail top rails and midrails must be at least 1/4 in in nominal diameter or thickness so they do not cut workers. A wire-rope top rail must be flagged with high-visibility material at intervals of no more than 6 ft.

Safety nets must be drop-tested at the jobsite after initial installation and before use, whenever they are relocated, after major repair, and every 6 months if left in one place. The test drops a 400 lb bag of sand, 30 in plus or minus 2 in in diameter, from the highest working surface, but from no less than 42 in above that level.

A full body harness must attach at the center of the wearer's back near shoulder level, or above the wearer's head. A body belt's attachment point is at the center of the back, but body belts may not be used for fall arrest.

Once erected with the line attached, warning-line stanchions must resist, without tipping over, a horizontal force of at least 16 lb applied 30 in above the surface, perpendicular to the line and toward the roof edge. The rope, wire or chain must have a minimum tensile strength of 500 lb.
Hole covers in roadways and vehicle aisles must support, without failure, at least twice the maximum axle load of the largest vehicle expected to cross them.

A shield system, usually called a trench box or trench shield, is a structure that withstands the forces of a cave-in and protects the workers inside it. Shields may be permanent or portable (moved along as work progresses) and either premanufactured or job-built, and unlike shoring they do not hold the trench walls in place.

Where oxygen deficiency (less than 19.5 percent oxygen) or a hazardous atmosphere exists or could reasonably be expected, such as in landfills or near stored hazardous substances, the air in an excavation must be tested before workers enter if it is more than 4 ft deep.

facts.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, Appendix A (manual tests)
facts.fact: In the plasticity test, soil that can be rolled into a 1/8 in thread at least 2 in long and held by one end without tearing is cohesive. In the thumb penetration test, Type A soil (about 1.5 tsf) can be readily indented by the thumb but penetrated only with great effort, while Type C soil (about 0.5 tsf) is easily penetrated several inches and molded with light finger pressure.

facts.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, Appendix A(b)
facts.fact: Type A soil is cohesive soil with an unconfined compressive strength of 1.5 tsf or more, such as clay, silty clay, sandy clay, clay loam, and cemented soils like caliche and hardpan. No soil is Type A if it is fissured, subject to vibration from heavy traffic or pile driving, previously disturbed, part of a layered system dipping into the excavation at 4H:1V or steeper, or otherwise less stable.

facts.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, Appendix A(b)
facts.fact: Type B cohesive soil has an unconfined compressive strength greater than 0.5 tsf but less than 1.5 tsf. Type C has 0.5 tsf or less and includes granular soils such as gravel, sand and loamy sand, submerged soil, and soil from which water is freely seeping.

facts.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, Appendix B (Figure B-1)
facts.fact: In Type A soil, excavations 20 ft deep or less may be sloped at 3/4H:1V, but short-term excavations (open 24 hours or less) that are 12 ft deep or less may be sloped at 1/2H:1V. Excavations 8 ft deep or less may have an unsupported vertical lower portion no taller than 3-1/2 ft.

Formwork must be designed, built, braced and maintained to support every vertical and lateral load that can reasonably be expected. Drawings or plans, including all revisions, for the jack layout, formwork and shoring, working decks and scaffolds must be available at the jobsite.

In multi-story steel erection, unless the design itself maintains structural integrity, there may be no more than 8 stories between the erection floor and the uppermost permanent floor, and no more than 4 floors or 48 ft (whichever is less) of unfinished bolting or welding above the foundation or uppermost permanently secured floor. Separately, a fully planked or decked floor or nets must always be kept within 2 stories or 30 ft (whichever is less) directly below any erection work; that rule has no design exception.
facts.reviewed: Design exception attached to the 2-story/30-ft decked floor or net rule; in 1926.754(b) it applies only to (b)(1) and (b)(2)

facts.fact: A bundle of joist bridging landed on steel joists may weigh no more than 1,000 lb in total. It must rest on at least 3 joists that are secured at one end, with the edge of the bundle within 1 ft of the secured end.

In underground construction the employer must provide safe access and egress to all work stations and protect workers from being struck by excavators, haulage machines, trains and other mobile equipment. Unused chutes, manways and other openings must be tightly covered, bulkheaded or fenced off and posted with Keep Out signs, and completed or unused sections must be barricaded.

Portable ladders, self-supporting or not, must hold at least 4 times their maximum intended load, except extra-heavy-duty Type 1A metal or plastic ladders, which must hold at least 3.3 times. For non-self-supporting ladders the load capacity is checked with the ladder set at 75-1/2 degrees from horizontal.

A non-self-supporting ladder is set so the horizontal distance from its top support to its foot is about one-quarter of its working length (a 4-to-1 ratio). A ladder with 16 ft of working length, for example, has its foot about 4 ft out from the support.
Workers must face the ladder when climbing up or down, keep at least one hand on it while moving, and not carry any object or load that could make them lose their balance.

A competent person does the crane shift inspection, a visual check for obvious deficiencies before or during each shift, with no disassembly or booming down unless the visual check or a trial run shows a need. It covers control mechanisms, pressurized lines, hydraulic fluid level, hooks and latches, wire rope and reeving, electrical apparatus, tires, ground conditions, level position, cab windows, and safety devices and operational aids.

Scaffolds may be erected, moved, dismantled or altered only under the supervision and direction of a competent person qualified in that work. Only experienced, trained employees chosen by that competent person may do the work.
Each employee who will enter a permit-required confined space, or that employee's authorized representative, must be given the chance to observe the pre-entry atmospheric testing.

facts.source: Earthwork estimating fundamentals (swell and load factor)
facts.fact: The load factor converts loose volume back to bank volume and equals 1 divided by (1 + swell). Soil with 25 percent swell has a load factor of 1/1.25 = 0.80, so 10 loose cubic yards equal 8 bank cubic yards.

To figure truck trips, convert bank cubic yards to loose cubic yards and divide by the truck's capacity, rounding up. For example, 1,000 BCY of soil with 32 percent swell is 1,000 x 1.32 = 1,320 LCY, and with 14 LCY trucks that is 1,320 / 14 = 94.3, so 95 trips.

facts.source: Earthmoving equipment practice (Peurifoy, Construction Planning, Equipment and Methods)
facts.fact: Scraper load time can be shortened by loading downgrade and by using push tractors (pusher dozers). The pusher pushes the scraper through the cut and boosts it as it leaves, which raises the loading rate.
In route and site layout, one full station is 100 ft and is written 1+00. Station 12+50 is therefore 1,250 ft along the baseline from the starting point at 0+00.

facts.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1926 Subpart P, Appendix D; trench shoring practice
facts.fact: Aluminum hydraulic shoring (hydraulic shoring jacks) can be installed and removed from the top of the trench, so workers do not have to enter an unprotected trench. It works best in firm soil that will stand long enough for the shores to be placed.

facts.source: ASTM D698 (standard Proctor); ASTM D1557 (modified Proctor)
facts.fact: The standard Proctor test (ASTM D698) compacts soil in a mold in 3 layers with a 5.5 lb rammer dropped 12 in, using 25 blows per layer in the 4 in mold (56 blows in the 6 in mold). The modified Proctor test (ASTM D1557) uses a 10 lb rammer dropped 18 in on 5 layers, which gives a higher compactive effort.
facts.reviewed: 25 blows per layer applies to the 4-in mold only; the 6-in mold uses 56 blows

facts.source: ASTM D698 / D1557; soil compaction fundamentals
facts.fact: The Proctor test plots dry density against moisture content to find a soil's maximum dry density and optimum moisture content. Field compaction is then specified and tested as a percentage of that maximum, such as 95 percent of standard Proctor.
Wellpoints lift water by suction, so a single stage can lower the water table only about 15 to 20 ft. Deeper drawdowns need multiple stages of wellpoints, or deep wells or ejectors.

Groundwater in an excavation is controlled by pumping from sumps, by perimeter ditches or trenches that drain to sumps and pumps, or by lowering the water table ahead of digging with wellpoints or deep wells.

A high groundwater table raises the contractor's excavation and foundation costs for dewatering and waterproofing. It also lowers soil bearing capacity, which affects the size and type of foundation the designer must use.

In post-tensioned concrete the tendons are not stressed until the concrete reaches the strength the engineer specifies, commonly about 75 percent of design strength (often around 3,000 psi). Until then neither the concrete nor the tendons carry any prestress.

A member is fully prestressed when no tensile stress develops under service (working) loads, and partially prestressed when some tension is allowed, with bonded mild reinforcement added to control crack width. Partial prestressing is the most common and economical approach.

facts.source: PTI Specification for Unbonded Single Strand Tendons
facts.fact: An unbonded single-strand tendon is a seven-wire steel strand coated with a corrosion-inhibiting post-tensioning coating (grease) and enclosed in plastic sheathing extruded around it. The strand can move relative to the concrete and is anchored only at its ends.

Post-tensioning jacks and their gauges are calibrated as a matched set and must stay together, and the numbers on the jack and gauge are checked against the calibration records. Stressing equipment is used only by trained personnel and only for stressing tendons.

facts.source: PTI / PT supplier handling and storage guidance
facts.fact: Post-tensioning tendons should be unloaded with nylon straps close to their storage area and stored dry and off the ground. Tarps over them are rigged like a tent so air circulates and condensation does not corrode the strand, and anchors and wedges are kept clean and dry.
facts.note: Supplier and PTI field guidance, not a code requirement; specific handling methods vary by supplier.

facts.fact: Post-tensioning installation drawings typically show tendon support bars about 4 ft on center. Extra supports may be needed so the tendon does not take a reverse curvature, which can cause the concrete to spall during stressing.
facts.note: From PT supplier installation guidance on the card; actual support spacing is set by the project shop drawings and specification.

facts.source: PTI barrier cable guidance (project specification governs)
facts.fact: For post-tensioned vehicle barrier cables, the non-stressing (dead-end) anchorage is commonly pre-seated, and the cable stressed, to about 80 percent of the strand's ultimate strength.
facts.note: The card's 80 percent of ultimate strength matches some barrier-cable guidance, but the exact seating and stressing forces come from the project specification and supplier; not confirmed.

facts.fact: By particle size, boulders are larger than 12 in and cobbles are 3 to 12 in. Gravel runs from 3 in down to the No. 4 sieve (about 3/16 in, 4.75 mm), sand from the No. 4 down to the No. 200 sieve (0.075 mm), and silt and clay are the fines that pass the No. 200 sieve.

facts.source: AASHTO M 146 soil terms; USDA texture classes; ASTM D2487
facts.fact: Clay particles are generally defined as finer than 0.002 mm, and silt as 0.002 to 0.075 mm (AASHTO; USDA uses 0.05 mm as the upper limit). The Unified system tells silt from clay by plasticity rather than particle size.
facts.note: Card gives silt as 0.002 to 0.02 mm, which is the International (Atterberg) scale. U.S. engineering practice puts the silt/sand boundary at the No. 200 sieve (0.075 mm).

facts.fact: Concrete sidewalks are typically 4 in thick, with a light broom finish and edges rounded with an edging tool. Contraction (control) joints are commonly spaced at about the width of the walk, roughly 4 to 5 ft.

A haul unit's cycle time is load, haul, dump and return time. Travel speeds depend on haul distance, rolling resistance, grade resistance (or grade assistance downhill), and the rimpull the machine can deliver.

Excavation walls are kept from caving either by sloping them back to a stable angle or with temporary earth support, such as interlocking steel sheet piling, steel soldier piles with horizontal timber lagging, or concrete slurry walls.

Underpinning gives an existing building new permanent support by extending its foundations down to a deeper bearing stratum. It is typically needed when nearby excavation will remove supporting soil or when new loads are added to the structure.

End-bearing piles carry load down to a firm stratum at the pile tip, friction piles carry it through skin friction along the shaft, and many piles use a combination of both. Piles are made of timber, steel, concrete or composite materials.

A pile's head is the top that takes the hammer blows, protected by a driving cap or, on timber piles, a steel pile ring that keeps it from brooming. On a tapered pile the butt is the large end and the tip the small end, a pile shoe is a metal point that protects the tip, and the cutoff is the part trimmed off after driving.

Standard holes for structural bolts are 1/16 in larger than the bolt diameter for bolts up to 7/8 in, so a 3/4 in bolt gets a 13/16 in hole. For bolts 1 in and larger the hole is 1/8 in larger, so a 1 in bolt gets a 1-1/8 in hole.
facts.note: Card says holes are always 1/16 in larger. AISC Table J3.3 uses bolt diameter plus 1/16 in only for bolts smaller than 1 in. A 1 in bolt gets a 1-1/8 in hole, and larger bolts get diameter plus 1/8 in.

facts.fact: Common hot-rolled steel shapes are W (wide flange), S (American Standard beam), C and MC (channels), L (equal- or unequal-leg angles), HP (bearing piles), WT and ST tees cut from W and S shapes, HSS (hollow structural sections) and plate. A W12x26 is a wide flange with a nominal depth of 12 in that weighs 26 lb per foot.

Common truss types include king post, queen post, Fink (W), Howe, Pratt, Warren, scissors, bowstring, Belgian and sawtooth. Under gravity load a Pratt truss has its diagonals in tension and verticals in compression, and a Howe truss is the reverse.

Tension cross-bracing (X-bracing) in steel frames handles load reversals because whichever diagonal is in tension resists the lateral load. The slender diagonals cannot resist compression, so removing one brace leaves the frame unstable for loads from that direction.

Girder-to-column connections are either simple (pin-type) shear connections or moment connections. Pin-type connections carry vertical load only and need cross-bracing, shear walls or a concrete core for lateral stability, while moment connections resist rotation between girder and column and give the frame its own lateral stability.
During steel erection, ironworkers line up the holes in connection plates and angles with drift pins and spud wrenches (wrenches with tapered handles) before final bolting.

The main types of steel deck are roof deck, form deck (a permanent form for concrete), composite floor deck (embossed so it bonds with the concrete and serves as the positive reinforcement), and cellular deck. Cellular deck has a flat bottom plate that forms cells used as electrical and communications raceways.
Steel deck sheets are made in cover widths commonly from about 24 to 36 in (some cellular and specialty decks are narrower), and are cut to length for the project, often spanning several supports.
facts.note: Card lists 12, 18, 24, 30 or 36 in as sheet lengths 'less than 40 in'. Those figures describe panel widths, not lengths, and exact widths vary by manufacturer and profile.

facts.source: Concrete construction practice (two-way joist systems, ACI 318)
facts.fact: A waffle slab is a two-way joist system formed with domes. The positive (bottom) reinforcement is concentrated in the ribs, while the negative reinforcement and temperature steel are placed within the slab thickness.
Stucco is exterior portland cement plaster. Over metal or wire lath it is applied in three coats (scratch, brown and finish) totaling about 7/8 in, and over masonry or concrete in at least two coats.

EPDM is a thermoset (rubber) single-ply membrane, so its seams cannot be heat-welded and are made by lapping with splice adhesive or seam tape. Thermoplastic membranes such as PVC and TPO are joined by heat welding.

A curtain wall is a non-load-bearing exterior wall that carries only its own weight and lateral (wind) loads to the building frame. A masonry wall that carries floor or roof loads is a bearing wall, not a curtain wall.
facts.note: Card says masonry curtain walls are either load-bearing or non-load-bearing. By definition a curtain wall carries no floor or roof loads; the load-bearing/non-load-bearing split describes masonry walls in general.

facts.source: IBC 2021 Chapter 7 (fire-resistance of structural members); fireproofing practice
facts.fact: Structural steel is fireproofed with spray-applied fire-resistive materials, intumescent coatings, concrete or masonry encasement, or gypsum board enclosures. Lightweight insulating (cellular) concrete works well because its low density and high insulating value slow heat transfer.

Stirrups are U-shaped or closed bars placed vertically across a beam to resist diagonal tension caused by shear. Shear is greatest near the supports, so stirrups are spaced closer together there and farther apart toward midspan.

Concrete is strong in compression but weak in tension, with a tensile strength of roughly one-tenth of its compressive strength. Reinforcing steel is therefore placed wherever tension occurs, such as near the bottom of a simply supported beam.

In structural slabs, shrinkage and temperature (T&S) reinforcement runs at right angles to the main flexural steel to control cracking from drying shrinkage and temperature change. Deformed T&S bars may be spaced no farther apart than five times the slab thickness or 18 in, whichever is less.

ASTM A615 inch-pound bar designations run #3 through #11, plus #14, #18 and the less common #20, the largest bar in the specification. The soft-metric designations (#10, #13, #16, #19, #22, #25, #29, #32, #36, #43, #57, #64) give the approximate diameter in millimeters, so a #5 bar (5/8 in) is a metric #16.
facts.reviewed: Current ASTM A615 also includes the No. 20 [64] bar, so '11 sizes' is wrong for the cited standard

facts.fact: When concrete is placed, reinforcing steel must be free of mud, oil and other coatings that impair bond. Normal rust and mill scale are acceptable as long as a hand-wire-brushed sample still meets the ASTM minimum dimensions, weight and deformation height.
facts.note: Card lists mill scale and rust among the conditions that decrease bond, then says rust improves bond. Under ACI, ordinary rust and mill scale are not grounds for rejection if a wire-brushed specimen meets ASTM minimums; only mud, oil and other deleterious coatings must be removed.

facts.source: ACI 318-19 Table 20.5.1.3.1 (specified concrete cover, cast-in-place nonprestressed)
facts.fact: Minimum cover for cast-in-place nonprestressed concrete is 3 in where cast against and permanently exposed to earth (such as footing bottoms); where exposed to weather or in contact with ground it is 2 in for #6 and larger bars and 1-1/2 in for #5 and smaller. Where not exposed, slabs, walls and joists need 3/4 in for #11 and smaller bars, and beams and columns need 1-1/2 in over primary bars, ties, stirrups and spirals.
facts.note: Card gives 3 in 'at sides' and 2 in for bars larger than #5 without stating the exposure conditions. In ACI 318 the 3-in cover applies to concrete cast against and permanently exposed to earth, and the 2-in / 1-1/2-in values apply to concrete exposed to weather or in contact with ground. The card's 3-in clearance for footing and mat bottom bars follows from the cast-against-earth rule.

facts.source: CRSI Placing Reinforcing Bars; CRSI tie types
facts.fact: The snap (single) tie is the simplest rebar tie and is used mainly on bars in flat horizontal work such as slabs. The wrap-and-snap tie is normally used on vertical wall reinforcement, saddle ties typically fasten column ties to corner bars and beam stirrups to corner bars, and the wrap-and-saddle tie (wire wrapped 1-1/2 times around the first bar) grips more firmly, as for heavy mats lifted by crane. The figure-eight tie may be used on walls in place of saddle or wrap-and-snap ties and also to secure heavy mats.
facts.reviewed: Claim that figure-eight tie is quicker but weaker than a saddle tie is unsupported; CRSI says it substitutes for saddle or wrap-and-snap ties and secures heavy mats

facts.source: CRSI Placing Reinforcing Bars (handling and hoisting)
facts.fact: Long bundles of reinforcing bars (roughly 30 ft and longer) are usually hoisted with a spreader beam so the bundle stays level and does not sag or slip; one handbook figure calls for the spreader to be at least half the bundle length.
facts.note: Industry handbook guidance (CRSI), not a code requirement; the 30-ft and one-half-length figures could not be confirmed against a current edition.

facts.source: CRSI Placing Reinforcing Bars (tying wall bars)
facts.fact: For a single curtain of wall reinforcement, one placing handbook calls for at least three ties on any one bar, with ties no more than about 4 to 6 ft apart in each direction; the actual number depends on bar size and spacing.
facts.note: Handbook (CRSI) tying guidance; the exact figures could not be confirmed, and project specifications govern.

facts.source: CRSI Manual of Standard Practice (bar supports)
facts.fact: Bottom bars in formed slabs are typically supported on continuous slab bolsters (SB), a wire bar support commonly supplied in 5-ft lengths; individual supports such as joist chairs and high chairs are used elsewhere.
