facts.note: Card lists slab bolster stock lengths of 2.5, 5 and 10 ft. CRSI standard practice shows 5-ft slab bolster lengths; other lengths appear to be manufacturer-specific, so the card's list could not be confirmed.

facts.fact: Roof underlayment keeps the sheathing dry until the roof covering goes on, acts as a secondary water barrier if wind-driven rain gets past the roofing, and separates asphalt shingles from resin pockets in wood sheathing that can damage them. It also cushions heavy coverings such as tile and slate.

Roof slope is the rise in inches per 12 in of horizontal run (slope = total rise x 12 / total run), so a 6-ft rise over a 12-ft run is 6 in 12 (6:12). Pitch is total rise divided by total span (twice the run), so a 6:12 slope is a 1/4 pitch.

Exposure is the part of a shingle left to the weather, top lap is the shingle width minus the exposure, and head lap is the overlap where three layers exist, equal to top lap minus exposure (width minus twice the exposure). For a 12-in strip shingle at 5-in exposure, top lap is 7 in and head lap is 2 in.

facts.source: ASTM D6380 Class WS (wide-selvage roll roofing); roofing practice
facts.fact: Double-coverage (19-in selvage) roll roofing comes in 36-in-wide rolls with a 17-in mineral-surfaced portion left exposed and a 19-in smooth selvage that the next course covers, so the roof has two layers throughout.

In a built-up roof the base sheet is the first ply installed, typically a heavier coated felt that may be mechanically fastened over nailable decks or insulation before the remaining plies are mopped in.
facts.note: Card says base sheets weigh 45 to 80 lb per square and that the base sheet acts as the vapor retarder protecting the insulation. Base sheet weights vary by product, and a vapor retarder is normally a separate layer on the warm side below the insulation, so these claims could not be confirmed.

facts.source: ASTM E96 (water vapor transmission); building science practice
facts.fact: A vapor retarder slows the diffusion of water vapor into an assembly (in cold climates, from the warm, humid interior) so it does not condense on cold surfaces inside the wall or roof. It is not the same as an air barrier, although a sealed sheet such as polyethylene can serve as both. Vapor resistance is rated in perms (1 perm = 1 grain of water vapor per sq ft per hour per inch of mercury vapor-pressure difference), and a lower perm rating means a better retarder.
facts.reviewed: Conflated vapor retarder (diffusion control) with air barrier (air leakage control)

facts.source: IRC 2021 R202 (vapor retarder class); IRC 2021 R702.7
facts.fact: The IRC classes vapor retarders by ASTM E96 desiccant-method permeance: Class I is 0.1 perm or less (e.g., polyethylene sheet, unperforated foil), Class II is more than 0.1 up to 1.0 perm (e.g., kraft-faced batts), and Class III is more than 1.0 up to 10 perm (e.g., latex or enamel paint).
Gutter hangers (strap, spike-and-ferrule or hidden clip types) are commonly spaced about 3 ft on center, and closer (roughly 18 in to 2 ft) where heavy snow or ice loads are expected.
facts.note: Trade and manufacturer guidance, not a code rule; recommended spacing varies by manufacturer and region.

facts.fact: The main steel deck types are roof deck (supports insulation and roofing), form deck (a non-composite permanent form for a reinforced concrete slab), composite floor deck (embossments lock it to the concrete so the deck acts as the slab's tension reinforcement), and cellular deck (a flat bottom sheet joined to fluted deck to form cells used as wiring raceways).

facts.source: SDI Manual of Construction with Steel Deck
facts.fact: Steel deck panels are commonly made in coverage widths of about 24 to 36 in and lengths up to roughly 40 ft, and one erection guide cites a maximum bundle weight of about 4,000 lb.
facts.note: Card lists widths of 12 to 36 in, 40-ft shipping lengths and a 4,000-lb bundle limit; these are manufacturer and handbook figures that vary by profile and supplier and could not be confirmed.

facts.fact: Steel deck should have at least 1-1/2 in of end bearing on its supports unless the design shows otherwise; where bearing is shorter, the designer must check the deck's end capacity and extra fastening may be required.

Steel deck is fastened to the structural frame with arc spot (puddle) welds, self-drilling screws (commonly #12 or #14, about 1/4 in) or powder-actuated or pneumatic pins. Screw guns use a clutch and depth-limiting nosepiece, and pneumatic tools run at a regulated pressure, to prevent over- or under-driving.

Small penetrations through steel deck (about 6 in, removing one rib) may need no reinforcing or only a light plate, somewhat larger holes get thicker reinforcing plates, and large openings must be framed with members extending past the opening as designed by the project engineer.
facts.note: Card gives a specific schedule (0.045-in and 0.057-in plates, framing above 13 in) and a C4x5.4 frame detail for 24-in openings; these are handbook or manufacturer details, not code, so the figures could not be confirmed.

facts.fact: IBC construction types: Types I and II have building elements of noncombustible materials; Type III has noncombustible exterior walls with interior elements of any permitted material; Type IV-HT (heavy timber) has noncombustible exterior walls and solid or laminated heavy-timber interior elements without concealed spaces; Type V allows any permitted material. The 2021 IBC also adds mass-timber Types IV-A, IV-B and IV-C.

facts.source: IBC 2021 Section 406 (parking garages: clear height, vehicle barriers)
facts.fact: In parking garages, each floor level must have at least 7 ft of clear height in vehicle and pedestrian traffic areas. Vehicle barriers at least 2 ft 9 in high are required at drive lanes and parking spaces where the drop to the ground or surface below is more than 1 ft.

Fire protection may be omitted from the bottom flange of lintels, shelf angles and plates that span 6 ft 4 in or less, whether or not they are part of the primary structural frame, and from those that are not part of the primary structural frame regardless of span.

Sprinkler system alarm, supervisory and trouble signals must each be distinct and must be sent automatically to an approved supervising station or, where the fire code official approves, sound an audible signal at a constantly attended location.

Fire pump suction, discharge and bypass valves and the isolation valves on the backflow preventer must be supervised open by one of four methods: a central-station, proprietary or remote-station signaling service; a local signaling service that sounds at a constantly attended location; locking the valves open; or sealing them, with approved weekly recorded inspections, where they sit inside owner-controlled fenced enclosures.

Egress lighting on emergency power (required for at least 90 minutes) must start at an average of at least 1 footcandle with no point below 0.1 footcandle along the path of egress at floor level. It may decline to a 0.6-footcandle average and 0.06-footcandle minimum by the end of the duration, and the maximum-to-minimum uniformity ratio may not exceed 40:1.

Where a required accessible floor is four or more stories above or below a level of exit discharge, at least one of its required accessible means of egress must be an elevator. In fully sprinklered buildings, exceptions apply to floors at or above exit discharge that have a horizontal exit and to floors served by a code-compliant ramp.

Each area of refuge must provide one 30 x 48 in wheelchair space for every 200 occupants or portion thereof, based on the occupant load of the refuge area and the areas it serves. These spaces may not reduce the required egress width, and reaching any space may not require passing more than one adjoining wheelchair space.

Nothing may project into the required clear opening width of an egress door below 34 in above the floor, and projections between 34 and 80 in above the floor (such as panic hardware) may not exceed 4 in; door closers and door stops may be as low as 78 in.

Egress stair risers must be at least 4 in and no more than 7 in high, measured vertically between adjacent tread nosings, and rectangular treads must be at least 11 in deep. In Group R-3 and inside dwelling units the limits relax to a 7-3/4 in maximum riser and 10 in minimum tread.

Means-of-egress ramps may have a running slope no steeper than 1 vertical in 12 horizontal. The IBC text labels this an '8-percent slope', although 1/12 works out to about 8.33 percent. A walking surface counts as a ramp once its running slope is steeper than 1:20 (5 percent).
facts.note: Card equates 1:12 with 8%. That is the IBC's own rounded label in 1012.2, so exam answers may show either 8% or 8.33%; the exact value of 1:12 is 8.33%.
facts.reviewed: IBC 1012.2 itself writes '(8-percent slope)' for 1:12; note wrongly faults the card, and tutor should know both figures for open-book exams

facts.fact: Handrails on stairs and ramps must be at a uniform height of 34 to 38 in, measured above the stair tread nosings or above the finished surface of the ramp slope.

For open valleys on asphalt shingle roofs, metal valley lining must be at least 24 in wide and of an approved corrosion-resistant metal. Alternatively, two plies of mineral-surfaced roll roofing (ASTM D3909 or D6380) may be used, with the bottom ply 18 in wide and the top ply at least 36 in wide.
Minimum thicknesses for metal valley lining under asphalt shingles include aluminum 0.024 in, cold-rolled copper 0.0216 in, galvanized steel 0.0179 in (26 gauge) and high-yield copper 0.0162 in.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: public vs private owners; public procurement law
facts.fact: Public owners (federal, state and local agencies) build with taxpayer funds and must follow procurement statutes, typically advertised competitive sealed bidding with award to the lowest responsive and responsible bidder plus statutory bonds, while private owners may choose contractors however they like, including by negotiation. A developer is a private owner who builds to sell or lease and often holds the project only briefly.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: organizing the construction company
facts.fact: A decentralized construction firm pushes more decisions out to project and field staff, while a centralized firm (common among small contractors) keeps most decision-making authority at the home office. Narrower specialization lets each worker focus on fewer issues and work faster.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: work breakdown structure
facts.fact: A work breakdown structure (WBS) is a deliverable-oriented hierarchy that divides the total project scope into manageable work packages, each with a defined scope, a responsible person, and measurable duration, cost and resources.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: project delivery methods
facts.fact: In design-bid-build (traditional) delivery, the owner first hires a design professional to complete the drawings and specifications, then bids the finished design and signs a separate construction contract, usually with the low responsive bidder. The designer and the contractor have no contract with each other.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: project delivery methods
facts.fact: Under construction management at risk (CMAR), the construction manager advises the owner during design and then holds the trade contracts and carries cost risk, usually under a guaranteed maximum price (GMP). In agency CM, by contrast, the CM is only the owner's advisor.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: construction manager services
facts.fact: Typical construction manager preconstruction services include feasibility and site studies, design and constructability review, value engineering, cost estimating, scheduling, procurement of long-lead items, and splitting the work into bid (work) packages.

facts.source: Commissioning practice (ASHRAE Guideline 0); NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: project completion
facts.fact: Commissioning is a quality process that verifies and documents that building systems such as HVAC and controls, electrical and fire alarm are installed and perform as the owner's project requirements call for. Closeout and commissioning should be planned from the start of the job, and closeout often overlaps the owner's move-in and startup.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: project cost control
facts.fact: For project control, the accepted estimate (budget) is the cost baseline and the approved schedule is the time baseline; actual costs and progress are compared with them to catch variances early.

Each technical specification section lists the submittals required for that work (shop drawings, product data, samples, test reports, O&M manuals, warranties), while the general conditions and the Division 01 submittal procedures section set how submittals are prepared, routed and reviewed.

Contractors usually request progress payments monthly, commonly on AIA G702 (Application and Certificate for Payment) supported by the G703 continuation sheet, which lists work completed and materials stored for each schedule-of-values line.

The Davis-Bacon Act requires contractors and subcontractors on federally funded or federally assisted contracts over $2,000 for building, altering or repairing (including painting and decorating) public buildings or public works to pay laborers and mechanics at least the local prevailing wage rates and fringe benefits set by the U.S. Department of Labor.

facts.source: 29 CFR 5.5(a)(3)(ii); Copeland Anti-Kickback Act, 40 U.S.C. 3145; 29 CFR Part 3
facts.fact: On Davis-Bacon covered jobs, each contractor and subcontractor must submit a certified payroll for every week it performs work (DOL's optional Form WH-347 may be used), signed with a statement of compliance; the Copeland Anti-Kickback Act makes it illegal to force workers to give back any part of their pay.

facts.source: Walsh-Healey Act, 41 U.S.C. 6502; FAR 22.602; Service Contract Act, 41 U.S.C. 6702
facts.fact: Other federal contract wage laws cover non-construction work. The Walsh-Healey Public Contracts Act applies to federal contracts to manufacture or furnish goods above an inflation-adjusted dollar threshold ($20,000 under FAR 22.602 since October 1, 2025, up from $15,000) and requires minimum wage, overtime after 40 hours a week, and child-labor and safety rules. The Service Contract Act requires prevailing wages and fringe benefits on federal service contracts over $2,500. Federal construction work falls under Davis-Bacon instead.
facts.reviewed: Walsh-Healey threshold is an inflation-adjusted FAR figure; raised from $15,000 to $20,000 effective Oct 1, 2025

facts.source: Consumer Credit Protection Act Title III, 15 U.S.C. 1673-1674; 29 CFR Part 870
facts.fact: Federal law limits an ordinary wage garnishment to the lesser of 25% of the employee's disposable earnings or the amount by which weekly disposable earnings exceed 30 times the federal minimum hourly wage, and forbids firing an employee because his wages are garnished for any one debt. Child support, bankruptcy and tax levies follow different limits.

An OSHA emergency action plan must list the names or regular job titles of the people or departments employees can contact for more information about the plan and their duties under it. The employer must train enough people to assist an orderly evacuation and review the plan with each covered employee when it is first developed, when that employee's duties under it change, and whenever the plan changes.

facts.source: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1200(g)(2) and Appendix D (applied to construction by 1926.59)
facts.fact: Section 1 (Identification) of a Safety Data Sheet gives the product identifier used on the label, recommended uses and restrictions, and the name, address and telephone number of the manufacturer, importer or other responsible party, plus an emergency telephone number.

facts.source: IRS Schedule C (Form 1040) instructions; IRS Pub 334
facts.fact: A sole proprietorship pays no separate income tax: the owner reports business income and expenses on Schedule C filed with his Form 1040, and the net profit is taxed as the owner's ordinary income at individual rates, whether or not the money is withdrawn from the business.

A sole proprietor or general partner owes self-employment tax (Social Security and Medicare) when net earnings from self-employment are $400 or more for the year. It is figured on Schedule SE and filed with Form 1040 at a combined 15.3% (12.4% Social Security up to the annual wage base plus 2.9% Medicare), and half of it is deductible.

facts.source: Federal-state unemployment insurance program (FUTA, 26 U.S.C. 3301; state UI laws)
facts.fact: Unemployment insurance, run by each state and funded mainly by employer state unemployment and FUTA taxes, pays temporary weekly benefits to eligible workers who lose their jobs through no fault of their own, such as in a layoff. Workers' compensation, by contrast, pays for job-related injuries and illnesses.

COBRA lets employees and covered family members keep the employer's group health coverage after a qualifying event; after job loss (other than for gross misconduct) or a cut in hours, coverage can continue for up to 18 months. It applies to employers with 20 or more employees, and the person can be charged up to 102% of the plan's cost.

facts.source: USCIS Form I-9 Lists of Acceptable Documents; 8 CFR 274a.2(b)(1)(v)(A)
facts.fact: A List A document proves both identity and employment authorization for Form I-9, so it is acceptable by itself. Examples are a U.S. passport or passport card, a Permanent Resident Card (Form I-551) and an Employment Authorization Document (Form I-766).

facts.source: USCIS Form I-9 Lists of Acceptable Documents; USCIS Handbook for Employers M-274
facts.fact: A Certificate of Naturalization (Form N-550/N-570) or Certificate of U.S. Citizenship (Form N-560/N-561) is not on the current Form I-9 lists of acceptable documents, so an employer may not accept one to verify employment eligibility.
facts.note: Card treats a Certificate of Naturalization as a document that establishes eligibility to work. These certificates were dropped from the acceptable-documents lists (reflected in the Form I-9 revised in 2007). A naturalized citizen can present a U.S. passport, or a List B identity document together with a List C document such as an unrestricted Social Security card.

facts.source: Uniform Partnership Act / Revised Uniform Partnership Act (dissociation and dissolution)
facts.fact: A general partnership lacks the perpetual life of a corporation: a partner's death or withdrawal can end the business unless the partnership agreement or state law lets the remaining partners continue and buy out the departing partner's interest, so a written agreement should include buy-sell terms.

facts.source: ISO commercial general liability form CG 00 01, Coverage A exclusions e (employer's liability) and j (damage to property)
facts.fact: A standard CGL policy pays only for bodily injury and property damage to third parties. It excludes injuries to the contractor's own employees (workers' compensation/employer's liability) and damage to property the contractor owns, rents or occupies, such as its own equipment and purchased materials (an equipment floater or builder's risk covers those), and any per-occurrence deductible is subtracted from the covered loss.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: business organization; state business corporation statutes
facts.fact: A C corporation's advantages include continuous (perpetual) existence regardless of changes in shareholders and easy transfer of ownership through shares; its disadvantages include higher costs to form and run, required formalities (articles, bylaws, a board of directors, meetings and minutes, annual reports) and heavier regulation and recordkeeping.

A C corporation may have any number of shareholders, but an S corporation may have no more than 100 shareholders (members of a family can count as one), may issue only one class of stock, and generally may not have corporations, partnerships or nonresident aliens as shareholders.

facts.source: Accounting fundamentals (statement of cash flows, indirect method)
facts.fact: Depreciation is a noncash expense: it reduces reported net income and taxable income without any cash leaving the business in that period, so it is added back to net income when figuring cash flow from operations.

Under the FLSA, the overtime premium is the extra half-time pay on hours over 40 in a workweek, while the full overtime rate is 1.5 times the regular rate. Example: $10/hr for 50 hours gives a premium of 10 hours x $5 = $50 and total gross pay of 50 x $10 + $50 = $550.

facts.source: NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: project management roles
facts.fact: In the NASCLA guide's description of project roles, the project manager is responsible for monitoring the project's compliance with building and safety codes.
facts.note: Based on the practice-test answer key, not confirmed against the guide text. On real jobs this duty is shared: the superintendent and safety staff enforce day-to-day compliance on site and the building official inspects, with the PM overseeing at the project level.

facts.fact: A partnership must file Form 1065 (U.S. Return of Partnership Income) every year, due by the 15th day of the 3rd month after its tax year ends (March 15 for a calendar year), and give each partner a Schedule K-1. It is an information return: the partnership pays no federal income tax itself, and the partners pay tax on their shares.
facts.note: Card says partnerships are the one business type that need not file an annual income tax return. A partnership does not pay federal income tax, but it must still file Form 1065 each year and faces a per-partner, per-month penalty for filing late.

facts.fact: Total float for an activity equals its late finish minus its early finish (or late start minus early start). An activity that can finish as early as day 20 but need not finish until day 26 has 6 days of float.

facts.source: IRS: Business Taxes (income, estimated, self-employment, employment, excise); state and local property tax law (e.g. Tenn. Code 67-5-901)
facts.fact: The IRS groups federal business taxes into income tax, estimated tax, self-employment tax, employment taxes and excise taxes. Property tax is not a federal tax, but state and local governments levy it, and businesses owning real estate (and in many states equipment and other tangible business personal property) must pay it.
facts.note: Card says property tax is generally not a business tax. It is not one of the federal business tax categories, but businesses routinely owe state/local property tax on real property and, in many states including Tennessee, on tangible business personal property.

facts.fact: A job description should set out the position's duties and responsibilities, required skills and knowledge, qualifications such as licenses or certifications, and reporting relationships. Under the ADA, a written job description prepared before advertising or interviewing for the job counts as evidence of the job's essential functions.

IRS failure-to-deposit penalties on employment taxes are 2% for deposits 1 to 5 calendar days late, 5% for 6 to 15 days late, 10% for more than 15 days late (or for amounts paid directly to the IRS or with the return instead of deposited), and 15% for amounts still unpaid more than 10 days after the first IRS notice.

facts.source: Workers' compensation rating fundamentals (NCCI classification rates per $100 of payroll)
facts.fact: Workers' compensation premiums are figured by job classification: premium = (class payroll / 100) x the class rate per $100 of payroll, summed for all classes and then adjusted by the experience modification and any credits or discounts. For example, $200,000 of payroll at $3.50 per $100 = $7,000.

facts.source: CSI MasterFormat (2004 and later editions); CSI SectionFormat
facts.fact: Project manual technical specifications are organized by CSI MasterFormat, which since the 2004 edition uses 50 divisions numbered 00 to 49 (replacing the old 16-division format). CSI SectionFormat arranges each specification section in three parts: Part 1 General, Part 2 Products and Part 3 Execution.

facts.source: AIA A201-2017 1.2.1 and 3.2.2; NASCLA Contractor's Guide topic: plans and specifications
facts.fact: When drawings and specifications conflict, the NASCLA guide teaches following the stricter (more demanding) requirement; in practice the contract's order-of-precedence clause controls, and the contractor should report the conflict to the architect and get a written clarification.
facts.note: Contract dependent. AIA A201-2017 1.2.1 treats the contract documents as complementary with no order of precedence, and 3.2.2 requires the contractor to report inconsistencies it finds; many general conditions say specifications govern over drawings or that the more stringent requirement applies.

facts.fact: A force majeure clause excuses a party from liability for delay or non-performance caused by events beyond its reasonable control, such as labor strikes, severe natural disasters, war, epidemics or government action; depending on its wording it usually grants a time extension rather than extra money.

facts.source: Construction contract law fundamentals (directed and constructive acceleration)
facts.fact: Schedule acceleration means requiring the contractor to finish sooner than the contract schedule allows. Directed acceleration is ordered by the owner; constructive acceleration occurs when the owner denies a time extension for an excusable delay and insists on the original date. In either case the contractor can generally recover its added costs.

facts.source: IRS Pub 15-A; IRS common-law rules (financial control)
facts.fact: Under the IRS financial-control factors, an employee is usually guaranteed a regular wage for each hour, week or other period, while an independent contractor is usually paid a flat fee or a time-and-materials price for the job (though some trades customarily bill hourly).

The purposes of marketing are to attract new customers, keep existing customers and generate repeat and referral work that raises sales and cash flow; recruiting and hiring employees is a human-resources function, not a marketing goal.

facts.source: IRS Pub 15-T (Federal Income Tax Withholding Methods)
facts.fact: IRS Pub 15-T gives two manual withholding methods: the wage bracket method (look up the pay-period wage in tables by filing status; covers wages up to about $100,000 a year) and the percentage method (works for any wage). Separate tables apply to Forms W-4 from 2020 or later, which use no allowances, and to older W-4s still on file that claim allowances; table amounts change every year.
facts.note: Card asks for withholding for a married employee with '3 exemptions' and gives $32 from an older Circular E table. Withholding tables now live in Pub 15-T and change annually, and the 2020 and later Form W-4 has no exemptions or allowances, so that dollar answer cannot be reused; always use the current year's tables.

facts.fact: An employee who believes the employer retaliated against him for a safety complaint or other activity protected by the OSH Act must file a Section 11(c) complaint with OSHA within 30 days of the retaliatory action.
I = E ÷ R = 120 ÷ 10 = 12 A. (Q: A 120-volt circuit feeds a 10-ohm resistive load. What is the current? A: 12 A)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: 240 V × 20 A = 4,800 W. (Q: A 240-volt, 20-ampere resistive load uses how much power? A: 4,800 W)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: All 125 V through 250 V receptacles in dwelling bathrooms require GFCI protection. (Q: In a dwelling unit, 125-volt, 15- and 20-ampere receptacles in bathrooms must have: A: GFCI protection for personnel)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: Table 250.122 lists 12 AWG copper for a 20 A overcurrent device. (Q: Minimum copper equipment grounding conductor for a circuit protected by a 20 A overcurrent device: A: 12 AWG)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: Rate the OCPD at not less than the noncontinuous load plus 125% of the continuous load. (Q: A branch-circuit overcurrent device supplying a continuous load must be rated at least what percent of the continuous load? A: 125%)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: Receptacles are placed so no point is more than 6 ft from one (12 ft max between them). (Q: In dwelling living areas, no point along the floor line of a wall may be more than ___ from a receptacle. A: 6 ft)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: No point along the countertop wall line may be more than 24 in from a receptacle outlet. (Q: Kitchen wall countertops: receptacles are placed so no point along the wall line is more than ___ from a receptacle. A: 24 in)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: Two or more 20 A small-appliance branch circuits are required. (Q: How many 20-ampere small-appliance branch circuits are required at minimum in a dwelling kitchen area? A: Two)

facts.fact: Condition 1 at 0–150 V to ground requires 3 ft (900 mm). (Q: Minimum working-space depth in front of 120/240 V equipment (0–150 V to ground), Condition 1: A: 3 ft)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: Height is 2.0 m (6½ ft) or the height of the equipment, whichever is greater. (Q: Minimum headroom for working space about service equipment and panelboards: A: 6.5 ft)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: 12 AWG Cu is 25 A at 75 °C, but 240.4(D) limits its overcurrent protection to 20 A. (Q: Ignoring small-conductor rules, the 75 °C ampacity of 12 AWG copper in Table 310.16 is: A: 25 A)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: 14 AWG = 2.00, 12 AWG = 2.25, 10 AWG = 2.50 cubic inches. (Q: Box-fill volume allowance for each 12 AWG conductor: A: 2.25 in³)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: P = E × I × √3 (1.732) × power factor. (Q: True power in a balanced three-phase circuit equals: A: E × I × 1.732 × PF)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: Pipe 2½ in and smaller: ¼ in per foot. 3–6 in: ⅛ in per foot. (Q: Minimum slope for a 2-inch horizontal drainage pipe: A: 1/4 in per ft)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: Pipe from 3 to 6 inches requires ⅛ in per foot minimum. (Q: Minimum slope for a 4-inch horizontal drainage pipe: A: 1/8 in per ft)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: Trap seals are 2 in minimum, 4 in maximum (deeper allowed only where designed for it). (Q: A fixture trap must have a liquid seal of at least ___ and not more than ___. A: 2 in / 4 in)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: A lavatory is rated at 1 DFU. (Q: Drainage fixture unit value of a lavatory: A: 1)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: Over 80 psi static, an approved PRV must reduce pressure to 80 psi or less. (Q: When static water pressure exceeds ___, a pressure-reducing valve is required. A: 80 psi)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: Private lavatory faucets are limited to 2.2 gpm at 60 psi. (Q: Maximum flow rate for a private lavatory faucet: A: 2.2 gpm at 60 psi)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: The discharge terminates atmospherically not more than 6 in above the floor or waste receptor. (Q: A water heater relief valve discharge pipe that terminates near the floor must end no more than ___ above the floor. A: 6 in)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: 1.08 × 1,000 × 20 = 21,600 Btu/h. (Q: Sensible heat for 1,000 CFM with a 20 °F temperature difference: A: 21,600 Btu/h)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: 1 ton = 12,000 Btu/h (heat to melt one ton of ice in 24 hours). (Q: One ton of refrigeration equals: A: 12,000 Btu/h)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: Type I = small appliances (5 lb or less). Type II = high-pressure, Type III = low-pressure. Vehicle A/C falls under Section 609. (Q: EPA Section 608 Type I certification covers: A: Small appliances with 5 lb or less of refrigerant)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: The venting prohibition took effect July 1, 1992. (Q: Knowingly venting ozone-depleting refrigerant during service became illegal on: A: July 1, 1992)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: Fill to no more than 80% to leave room for liquid expansion. (Q: A refillable recovery cylinder should not be filled beyond ___ of capacity by weight (liquid). A: 80%)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: Superheat = suction line temperature minus evaporator saturation temperature. (Q: Superheat is measured at the: A: Suction line leaving the evaporator)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: TXV systems are charged by subcooling; fixed-orifice systems by superheat. (Q: A system with a TXV is normally charged using: A: Subcooling)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: Not less than ⅛ in per foot (1% slope). (Q: Horizontal condensate drain piping must slope at least: A: 1/8 in per ft)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: As of January 1, 2020, R-22 may only come from recovered, recycled or stockpiled supply. (Q: Production and import of new R-22 ended in the U.S. on: A: January 1, 2020)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: Construction trigger height is 6 ft (scaffolds are 10 ft under 1926.451). (Q: Fall protection is required on construction walking/working surfaces with an unprotected edge ___ or more above a lower level. A: 6 ft)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: Side rails extend at least 3 ft above the upper landing surface. (Q: A portable ladder used to reach an upper landing must extend at least ___ above the landing. A: 3 ft)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: Excavations 5 ft or deeper need protection unless made entirely in stable rock. (Q: A protective system is required for trenches at what depth, unless in stable rock? A: 5 ft)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: Top edge height is 42 in plus or minus 3 in above the walking level. (Q: Top rail height of a guardrail system: A: 42 in ± 3 in)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: Maximum riser 7¾ in; minimum tread depth 10 in (R311.7.5.2). (Q: Maximum riser height for stairways in a one- or two-family dwelling: A: 7¾ in)

facts.fact: Handrails are not less than 34 in and not more than 38 in high. (Q: Handrail height on IRC stairways, measured from the tread nosing: A: 34–38 in)

facts.fact: 2 × 12 × 16 ÷ 12 = 32 board feet. (Q: How many board feet are in one 2 × 12 × 16 ft plank (nominal)? A: 32)

facts.fact: 30 × 20 × 0.333 = 200 ft³; 200 ÷ 27 = 7.4 yd³. (Q: A 30 ft × 20 ft slab, 4 in thick, needs about how much concrete before waste? A: 7.4 yd³)

facts.fact: $20,000 ÷ $100,000 = 20%. Markup would be $20,000 ÷ $80,000 = 25%. (Q: A job costs $80,000 and sells for $100,000. What is the gross profit margin? A: 20%)

facts.fact: Section 2 is due within 3 business days of the first day of employment. (Q: Employers must complete Section 2 of Form I-9 within ___ of the employee's first day of work. A: 3 business days)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: Form 941 is the Employer's Quarterly Federal Tax Return. Form 940 is annual FUTA. (Q: Federal income tax withheld and FICA taxes are reported on which IRS form, usually quarterly? A: Form 941)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: Payment bonds guarantee subs and suppliers get paid; performance bonds guarantee the work is completed. (Q: A payment bond on a construction project protects: A: Subcontractors and suppliers against nonpayment)

facts.fact: A stairway, ladder, ramp or other egress must be within 25 ft of lateral travel. (Q: Each job site with trenches 4 ft or deeper must have a means of egress within ___ of lateral travel. A: 25 ft)

facts.fact: A sole proprietor and the business are legally the same person, so the owner has unlimited personal liability. (Q: Which form of business leaves the owner personally liable for all of the company's debts? A: Sole proprietorship)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: An LLC limits members' personal liability while profits can pass through to the owners' personal returns. (Q: A contractor wants pass-through taxation but also wants personal assets protected from business debts. The best fit is usually: A: Limited liability company)

facts.fact: A valid contract needs offer and acceptance, consideration, capacity and a legal purpose. Notarization is not required. (Q: Which of these is NOT required for a contract to be legally valid? A: Notarization)

facts.fact: Contracts involving the sale of land or real property must be written to be enforceable. (Q: Under the statute of frauds, which contract must be in writing to be enforceable? A: A contract for the sale of real property)

facts.fact: A conditional waiver gives up lien rights only once the payment clears. An unconditional waiver is effective on signing, so only sign one after you are paid. (Q: A conditional lien waiver takes effect: A: Only after the stated payment is actually received)

facts.fact: Liquidated damages are a pre-agreed amount for late completion, set when actual damages would be hard to measure. (Q: A contract clause requiring the contractor to pay the owner $500 for each day the project finishes late is called: A: Liquidated damages)

facts.fact: If the winning bidder backs out, the bid bond covers the owner's cost of going to the next bidder, up to the bond amount. (Q: A bid bond guarantees that: A: The low bidder will sign the contract and provide the required bonds if awarded)

facts.fact: The Miller Act requires both bonds on federal construction contracts above the threshold set in the Federal Acquisition Regulation. Davis-Bacon covers prevailing wages. (Q: Which federal law requires performance and payment bonds on federal construction contracts? A: Miller Act)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: Builder's risk is property coverage for the structure and materials during construction. Employee injuries fall under workers' compensation. (Q: Builder's risk insurance primarily covers: A: Damage to the building and materials while under construction)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: Workers' comp is a no-fault system. In exchange, employees generally cannot sue the employer for covered injuries. (Q: Workers' compensation insurance pays benefits for job-related injuries: A: Regardless of who was at fault)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: Employer and employee each pay 6.2% for Social Security. Medicare is 1.45% each, so the combined FICA share per side is 7.65%. (Q: The employer's share of Social Security tax is ___ of each employee's wages, up to the annual wage base. A: 6.2%)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: Employer and employee each pay 1.45% for Medicare, with no wage cap. The extra 0.9% on high earners is withheld from the employee only. (Q: The employer's share of Medicare tax is: A: 1.45%)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: The FUTA wage base is the first $7,000 per employee each calendar year. It is reported annually on Form 940. (Q: Federal unemployment (FUTA) tax applies to the first ___ of wages paid to each employee per year. A: $7,000)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: The W-4 sets federal income tax withholding. Work authorization is verified on Form I-9, and annual wages are reported on Form W-2. (Q: An employee completes Form W-4 so the employer can: A: Figure how much federal income tax to withhold)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: The IRS weighs behavioral control, financial control and the relationship of the parties. The more the business controls how the work is done, the more likely the worker is an employee. (Q: When deciding whether a worker is an employee or an independent contractor, the IRS mainly looks at: A: The degree of control the business has over the work)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: Federal law requires at least 1.5 times the regular rate for hours over 40 in a workweek. Some states also require daily overtime. (Q: Under the Fair Labor Standards Act, a non-exempt employee must be paid overtime for hours worked over ___ in a workweek. A: 40)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: 40 × $20 = $800, plus 6 overtime hours × $30 (1.5 × $20) = $180, for a total of $980. (Q: A non-exempt carpenter earning $20 per hour works 46 hours in one workweek. Gross pay is: A: $980)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: Keep the I-9 for 3 years from the hire date or 1 year after employment ends, whichever is later. (Q: An employer must keep a former employee's Form I-9 for: A: 3 years after hire or 1 year after employment ends, whichever is later)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: The Form 300A summary of the prior year is posted from February 1 to April 30. (Q: Employers covered by OSHA recordkeeping must post the annual injury summary (Form 300A) from: A: February 1 to April 30)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: OSHA 300 logs, 300A summaries and 301 incident reports are kept for 5 years following the end of the calendar year they cover. (Q: OSHA injury and illness records must be kept for: A: 5 years after the end of the calendar year they cover)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: Fatalities are reported within 8 hours. In-patient hospitalization, amputation or loss of an eye is reported within 24 hours. (Q: A work-related fatality must be reported to OSHA within: A: 8 hours)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: Everything the business owns (assets) is financed either by creditors (liabilities) or by the owners (equity). (Q: The basic accounting equation is: A: Assets = Liabilities + Owner's equity)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: $250,000 ÷ $100,000 = 2.5. Working capital would be $250,000 − $100,000 = $150,000. (Q: A contractor has $250,000 in current assets and $100,000 in current liabilities. The current ratio is: A: 2.5)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: The quick ratio counts only assets that convert to cash fast, so inventory (and usually prepaid expenses) are left out. (Q: The quick (acid-test) ratio differs from the current ratio because it leaves out: A: Inventory)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: (Cost − salvage) ÷ useful life = ($50,000 − $10,000) ÷ 5 = $8,000 per year. (Q: A $50,000 truck with a $10,000 salvage value is depreciated straight-line over 5 years. Annual depreciation is: A: $8,000)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: $120,000 ÷ 0.20 = $600,000 in revenue before any net profit is earned. (Q: A contractor's annual overhead is $120,000 and jobs average a 20% gross profit margin. Revenue needed to break even is: A: $600,000)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: Target housing is housing built before 1978, when lead-based paint was banned for residential use. (Q: EPA's Lead Renovation, Repair and Painting (RRP) rule applies to work in housing built before: A: 1978)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: Firms must give the Renovate Right pamphlet and get written acknowledgment before work begins. (Q: Before starting an RRP-covered renovation in a pre-1978 home, the renovator must give the owner: A: EPA's Renovate Right pamphlet)
facts.note: From the hand-checked core question bank

facts.fact: A conditional lien waiver gives up lien rights only after the stated payment is actually received (it is conditioned on payment); an unconditional lien waiver is effective as soon as it is signed, so sign one only after the money has cleared.

In the IMC, an appliance is a manufactured device that uses energy and has specific code requirements (such as a furnace or boiler), while equipment means the permanently installed piping, ducts, vents, controls and other system components other than appliances.

A plenum is an enclosed part of the building structure, other than a conditioned occupiable space, that is designed to let air move through it so it serves as part of the air distribution system (for example, the space above a dropped ceiling used as a return).

'Access' means something can be reached but may first require removing an access panel, door or similar obstruction; 'ready access' means it can be reached directly without removing panels or doors and without portable ladders or similar equipment.

Environmental air is air moved to or from occupied areas through ducts that are not part of the heating or air-conditioning system, such as bathroom exhaust, domestic kitchen range exhaust, domestic clothes dryer exhaust and parking garage exhaust.
Makeup air is outdoor air brought into a building to replace air that is being exhausted.
A direct-vent appliance is built and installed so that all combustion air comes directly from outdoors and all flue gases discharge directly to outdoors; it does not use room air for combustion.

Commercial cooking appliances are grouped by duty: extra-heavy-duty appliances use solid fuel such as wood or charcoal; heavy-duty includes underfired broilers, chain (conveyor) broilers, gas open-burner ranges and wok ranges; medium-duty includes fryers, griddles, hot-top ranges and electric discrete-element ranges; light-duty includes ovens, steamers, kettles and pasta cookers.
facts.reviewed: Ranges are split: gas open-burner ranges are heavy-duty; only electric discrete-element and hot-top ranges are medium-duty. 'Medium-duty includes ranges' is misleading.

facts.fact: A refrigeration machinery room is a room that meets prescribed safety requirements and houses refrigeration systems or their components, such as compressors.
Appliances regulated by the IMC must be listed and labeled for the application in which they are installed and used, unless otherwise approved by the code official.

Equipment and appliances must be installed per their listing, the manufacturer's installation instructions and the code, and the manufacturer's installation instructions must be available on the job site at the time of inspection.

Fuel-fired appliances may not be located in sleeping rooms, bathrooms, toilet rooms, storage closets or surgical rooms, or in a space that opens only into those rooms, unless an exception applies, such as a direct-vent appliance or an appliance in a dedicated enclosure that takes all combustion air from outdoors and has a solid, weatherstripped, self-closing door.

Exceptions to the prohibited-location rule allow one wall-mounted unvented room heater with an oxygen depletion safety shutoff in a bathroom if it is 6,000 Btu/h or less, or in a bedroom if it is 10,000 Btu/h or less, provided the room meets the required volume for combustion air.

In garages (private, public, repair and parking garages) and hazardous locations, appliances with an ignition source must be elevated so the source of ignition (burner, igniter or switch) is at least 18 inches above the floor. Exception: elevation is not required for appliances listed as flammable vapor ignition resistant (FVIR).
facts.reviewed: Leaves out the exception that is tested most often: appliances listed as flammable-vapor-ignition-resistant (FVIR), such as most modern gas water heaters, do not have to be elevated.

facts.fact: In public garages, motor fuel-dispensing facilities and repair garages, appliances must be at least 8 ft above the floor; where vehicles can pass under the appliance, it must be at least 1 ft higher than the tallest vehicle garage door opening, unless protected from vehicle impact.
facts.note: Confirmed from ICC 2021 IMC Study Companion sample.

facts.fact: Appliances in private garages and carports must have at least 6 ft of clearance above the floor unless they are protected from motor vehicle impact and installed with the required 18 in ignition-source elevation.
facts.note: Confirmed from ICC 2021 IMC Study Companion sample.

facts.fact: Equipment installed at grade must sit on a level concrete slab or other approved material at least 3 inches above the adjoining grade, or be suspended at least 6 inches above grade.
Guards are required where equipment needing service, or a roof hatch, is within 10 ft of a roof edge or open side that is more than 30 inches above the floor, roof or grade below.

Rooftop equipment guards must extend at least 30 inches beyond each end of the equipment or hatch, have a top at least 42 inches above the adjacent surface, and be built so a 21-inch-diameter sphere cannot pass through.

Appliances must be accessible for inspection, service, repair and replacement without removing permanent construction or other appliances, and a level working space at least 30 inches deep and 30 inches wide must be provided in front of the control side.

Central furnaces in compartments or alcoves need at least 3 inches of working clearance along the sides, back and top, with the enclosure at least 12 inches wider than the furnace (6 inches at the front if the firebox is open to the atmosphere). Exception: replacement furnaces installed in existing compartments or alcoves may use the manufacturer's working clearances.
facts.reviewed: The exception is wrong. The 306.1.1 exception covers replacement furnaces in existing compartments or alcoves, which may use the manufacturer's clearances. It is not about a furnace 'listed for less clearance'.

facts.fact: Rooms containing appliances must have a door and an unobstructed passageway at least 36 inches wide and 80 inches high.

Inside a dwelling unit, an appliance in a compartment, alcove, basement or similar space may be reached through an opening or door and passageway at least 24 inches wide and large enough to remove the largest appliance, if a level service space at least 30 inches deep (and the appliance height, but not less than 30 in) is provided at the front with the door open.

Attics containing appliances need an opening and unobstructed passageway large enough to remove the largest appliance; the passageway must be at least 30 inches high and 22 inches wide and no more than 20 ft long measured along its centerline from the opening to the appliance.
facts.note: Confirmed from 2021 IMC text quoted in Brenham TX local amendment.

facts.fact: The attic passageway must have continuous solid flooring at least 24 inches wide, and a level service space at least 30 inches deep and 30 inches wide must be provided at the front or service side of the appliance.
The clear attic access opening serving an appliance must be at least 20 inches by 30 inches and large enough to remove the largest appliance.

The attic passageway and service space are not required if the appliance can be serviced and removed through the access opening; and where the passageway is unobstructed and at least 6 ft high and 22 inches wide for its whole length, it may be up to 50 ft long.
An attic containing an appliance must have a light fixture controlled by a switch at the passageway opening, and a receptacle outlet at or near the appliance location, installed per NFPA 70.

For appliances under floors (crawl spaces), the access opening must be at least 22 inches by 30 inches, and the passageway at least 30 inches high and 22 inches wide and no more than 20 ft long, with a 30 in by 30 in level service space at the appliance.
An under-floor passageway that is unobstructed and at least 6 ft high and 22 inches wide for its entire length is not limited in length.

Where the under-floor passageway or service space is excavated more than 12 inches below adjoining grade, its walls must be lined with concrete or masonry extending at least 4 inches above the adjoining grade.

A permanent interior or exterior means of access is required where a person would have to climb more than 16 ft above grade to reach rooftop or elevated equipment; the access route may not require climbing over obstructions over 30 inches high or walking on roofs steeper than 4:12 (33 percent slope).
Permanent exterior ladders providing roof access do not have to extend closer than 12 ft to the finished grade or floor below.
Permanent ladders for equipment access that are over 30 ft high must have offset sections with landings.
facts.note: Mentioned in ICC 2021 IMC study companion sample.

facts.fact: Permanent equipment-access ladders are required to have rungs spaced no more than 14 inches on center, at least 18 inches between rails, and at least 6 inches of toe clearance behind the rungs.
facts.note: Recalled values; could not confirm the full ladder list against 2021 text.

facts.fact: Where serviceable equipment is on a roof sloped 3:12 (25 percent) or steeper with an edge more than 30 inches above grade, a level platform at least 30 inches in every dimension, with guards, must be provided on each side of the equipment that needs service access.

A 125-volt, single-phase, 15- or 20-ampere receptacle must be installed at an accessible location within 25 ft of heating, air-conditioning and refrigeration equipment, on the same level, and it may not be connected to the load side of the equipment disconnect.
Spaces intended for human occupancy must have heating able to maintain at least 68 degrees F at a point 3 ft above the floor on the design heating day.
Heating and cooling design loads used to size systems and equipment must be determined using ASHRAE/ACCA Standard 183 or another approved method.
In one- and two-family dwellings, heating and cooling equipment must be sized using ACCA Manual S based on loads calculated with ACCA Manual J or another approved method.
Residential duct systems must be installed per ACCA Manual D, the appliance manufacturer's instructions, or other approved methods.
For residential load calculations, the interior design temperature may be no higher than 72 degrees F for heating and no lower than 75 degrees F for cooling.
facts.reviewed: IECC R302.1 sets limits, not fixed values: no higher than 72 F for heating and no lower than 75 F for cooling.

facts.fact: Ducts in an attached garage and ducts penetrating the walls or ceiling between the dwelling and the garage must be at least No. 26 gage sheet steel (or other approved material) and may have no openings into the garage.
Furnaces and air-handling systems that serve living spaces may not supply air to, or return air from, an attached garage.

Return air for a forced-air system may not be taken from a closet, bathroom, toilet room, kitchen, garage, mechanical room, boiler room, furnace room or unconditioned attic. Exceptions: a kitchen return is allowed if it serves only the kitchen and is at least 10 ft from the cooking appliances, and a dedicated forced-air system serving only a garage may take return air from the garage.
facts.reviewed: Since the 2018 IRC, M1602.2 covers return air only (outdoor air openings are in M1602.1). The list also leaves out 'mechanical room' and the exception for a dedicated garage-only system.

facts.fact: Outdoor air intakes for a forced-air system may not be closer than 10 ft to an appliance vent outlet, a plumbing vent or an exhaust fan discharge, unless the intake is at least 3 ft below that outlet.
facts.reviewed: Wrong section. Since the 2018 IRC, outdoor air intake openings are covered in M1602.1; M1602.2 covers return air.

facts.fact: Condensate drain lines must be at least 3/4 inch internal diameter and may not get smaller anywhere between the drain pan connection and the point of disposal.

When condensate drains from several units are manifolded together, size the common line by total cooling capacity: up to 20 tons 3/4 in; over 20 to 40 tons 1 in; over 40 to 90 tons 1-1/4 in; over 90 to 125 tons 1-1/2 in; over 125 to 250 tons 2 in.
Worked example: three 15-ton rooftop units manifolded to one condensate line total 45 tons, which falls in the over-40-to-90-ton row, so the shared line must be at least 1-1/4 inch.

Condensate from all cooling coils and fuel-burning condensing appliances must be carried from the drain pan outlet to an approved place of disposal and may not be discharged into a street, alley or other area where it would create a nuisance.
facts.reviewed: 307.2.1 covers cooling coils and evaporators. Condensate from fuel-burning condensing appliances is covered by 307.1.

facts.fact: Where an overflow of the primary condensate drain could damage building components, one of four protections is required: an auxiliary pan with its own drain, an overflow drain from the equipment pan, an auxiliary pan with a water-level shutoff switch, or a water-level shutoff device in the drain line or equipment pan.

An auxiliary (secondary) drain pan must be at least 1-1/2 inches deep, at least 3 inches larger than the unit or coil in both length and width, and made of corrosion-resistant material: at least 0.0236 in (No. 24 gage) galvanized steel or 0.0625 in thick if nonmetallic.

An auxiliary pan drain or overflow drain must discharge to a conspicuous point where occupants will notice it (for example, above a window), to warn that the primary drain is stopped; an overflow connection on the equipment pan must be higher than the primary drain connection.

Water-level detection devices used to shut down equipment on a blocked condensate drain must conform to UL 508; in a drain line or equipment pan, the device must sit above the primary drain connection and below the pan's overflow rim.

On down-flow units and other coils with no secondary drain or room for an auxiliary pan, a water-level device must be installed inside the primary drain pan; devices installed externally or in the drain line are not allowed for this case.
Fuel-fired appliances that automatically shut down when their condensate drainage system is blocked are exempt from the auxiliary drain protection requirements.
Condensate drains must be trapped as required by the equipment or appliance manufacturer.
Condensate drains for ductless mini-split equipment must have either an inline check valve in the drain line or a trap.
Condensate drain lines must be configured so blockages can be cleared and maintenance done without cutting the drain line (for example, with a cleanout tee).
A condensate pump in an uninhabitable space such as an attic or crawl space must be wired so that if the pump fails, the appliance or equipment it serves is prevented from operating.
facts.note: Requirement confirmed; subsection number differs between editions.

facts.fact: Every occupied space must be ventilated by natural means (IMC 402) or mechanical means (IMC 403).
Natural ventilation requires openable area to the outdoors (windows, doors, louvers) of at least 4 percent of the floor area being ventilated.

An interior room may be naturally ventilated through an adjoining room only if the unobstructed opening between them is at least 8 percent of the interior room's floor area and at least 25 square feet.

Mechanical outdoor-air intake openings must be at least 10 ft from lot lines and buildings on the same lot, and at least 10 ft horizontally from hazardous or noxious contaminant sources such as vents, chimneys, plumbing vents and parking lots.

An outdoor-air intake within 10 ft horizontally of a contaminant source must be at least 3 ft below that source; intakes may be closer to streets, alleys, parking lots and loading docks only if they are at least 25 ft above them.
Outdoor air intake openings must be screened; for residential occupancies the screen openings must be at least 1/4 inch and no larger than 1/2 inch.
Breathing-zone outdoor air is Vbz = (Rp x Pz) + (Ra x Az), where Rp is cfm per person, Pz is the number of people, Ra is cfm per square foot and Az is floor area.
Office space requires 5 cfm per person plus 0.06 cfm per square foot. Example: a 1,000 sq ft office with 5 people needs (5 x 5) + (0.06 x 1,000) = 25 + 60 = 85 cfm of breathing-zone outdoor air.

Classrooms for ages 9 and up use a default of 35 people per 1,000 sq ft, 10 cfm per person and 0.12 cfm per sq ft. Example: a 1,000 sq ft classroom with 35 students needs (10 x 35) + (0.12 x 1,000) = 470 cfm.

Zone outdoor airflow is Voz = Vbz / Ez, where Ez is air distribution effectiveness. Ez is 1.0 for cool air supplied from the ceiling, and 0.8 for warm air supplied at the ceiling at 15 F or more above space temperature with a ceiling return (warm air less than 15 F above space temperature can be 1.0). Example: 85 cfm / 0.8 = about 106 cfm.
facts.reviewed: The Ez of 0.8 for ceiling supply and return applies only when the warm supply air is 15 F or more above space temperature. Warm air less than 15 F above space temperature (with throw to within 4.5 ft of the floor) is 1.0.

facts.fact: Public toilet rooms need exhaust of 50 cfm per water closet or urinal if the fan runs continuously while occupied, or 70 cfm per fixture if it runs intermittently; private toilet rooms need 25 cfm continuous or 50 cfm intermittent.
Dwelling-unit local exhaust minimums: kitchens 100 cfm intermittent or 25 cfm continuous; bathrooms and toilet rooms 50 cfm intermittent or 20 cfm continuous.

The continuous whole-house ventilation rate may be taken from IRC Table M1505.4.3(1) or calculated with Equation 15-1: (0.01 x floor area in sq ft) + 7.5 x (bedrooms + 1). Example by equation: a 2,000 sq ft, 3-bedroom house needs 20 + 30 = 50 cfm.
facts.note: The table (by floor-area and bedroom ranges) can give a higher value than the equation for the same house.

facts.fact: Under the 2021 IRC, a dwelling unit tested at 5 air changes per hour or less at 50 Pascals (blower door) must be provided with whole-house mechanical ventilation (earlier editions said 'less than 5').
facts.reviewed: The 2021 IRC R303.4 threshold reads '5 air changes per hour or less' (earlier editions said 'less than 5').

facts.fact: Exhaust air must discharge outdoors where it will not be a nuisance or be drawn back into a ventilation intake, and may not be exhausted into an attic, soffit, ridge vent or crawl space.

Environmental air exhaust outlets (such as toilet and bath exhaust) must terminate at least 3 ft from property lines, at least 3 ft from operable openings into buildings, and at least 10 ft from mechanical air intakes.

Exhaust outlets for product-conveying systems (other than those conveying explosive or flammable materials) must be at least 10 ft from property lines, 3 ft from exterior walls and roofs, 10 ft from operable openings, and 10 ft above adjoining grade.

Exhaust outlets for ducts carrying explosive or flammable vapors, fumes or dusts must be at least 30 ft from property lines, 10 ft from operable openings, 6 ft from exterior walls and roofs, 30 ft from combustible walls or openings in the discharge direction, and 10 ft above grade.
facts.note: Recalled list; not confirmed against 2021 text.

facts.fact: Residential exhaust openings must terminate at least 3 ft from property lines, at least 3 ft from gravity air intakes and operable windows and doors, and at least 10 ft from mechanical air intakes unless the exhaust is at least 3 ft above the intake.
facts.reviewed: Wrong section. In the 2021 IRC, exhaust opening locations are in M1504.3; M1505 is mechanical ventilation.

facts.fact: Residential exhaust fans must discharge directly to the outdoors; they may not discharge into an attic, soffit, ridge vent or crawl space.

Clothes dryer exhaust must terminate outdoors, at least 3 ft from any opening into the building (including ventilated soffits) unless the dryer manufacturer says otherwise, and screens are not allowed at the termination.
Domestic dryer exhaust ducts must have a smooth interior finish, be made of metal at least 0.0157 inch thick (No. 28 gage), and be 4 inches nominal diameter.
facts.note: Older editions (2015 and earlier) stated 0.016 inch.
facts.reviewed: The 2018 and later IMC (504.8.1) and the IRC both require metal at least 0.0157 inch (No. 28 gage). The value 0.016 inch comes from older editions. The code also says 'metal', not 'rigid metal'.

facts.fact: Dryer exhaust duct joints must have the male (insert) end pointing in the direction of airflow, and screws or fasteners may not protrude more than 1/8 inch into the duct.
Domestic dryer exhaust ducts must be supported at intervals not exceeding 12 ft and secured in place.
facts.note: Older editions (2012 and earlier) required support at 4-ft intervals.
facts.reviewed: The current IMC 504.8.2 (and IRC M1502.4.2) requires dryer exhaust ducts to be supported at intervals of no more than 12 ft. The 4-ft interval is from older editions.

facts.fact: The transition duct connecting a dryer to the exhaust duct must be a single length no longer than 8 ft, listed and labeled to UL 2158A, and may not be concealed inside construction.
The maximum developed length of a domestic dryer exhaust duct is 35 ft, measured from the transition duct connection to the outlet terminal, reduced by the equivalent length of each fitting.
Dryer duct fitting deductions: 4-in-radius mitered 45-degree elbow 2 ft 6 in; 4-in-radius mitered 90-degree elbow 5 ft; 6-in-radius smooth 45 1 ft; 6-in-radius smooth 90 1 ft 9 in.
Worked example: a dryer duct with two 4-in-radius mitered 90-degree elbows and one mitered 45 may have at most 35 - (2 x 5) - 2.5 = 22.5 ft of straight duct.
A longer dryer exhaust duct is permitted when the make and model of the dryer are known and the manufacturer's installation instructions allow the longer length.
If the dryer duct equivalent length exceeds 35 ft, a permanent label or tag stating the duct's equivalent length must be placed within 6 ft of the exhaust duct connection.
Where a clothes dryer exhausts more than 200 cfm, makeup air must be provided; a dryer installed in a closet needs an opening of at least 100 square inches for makeup air.
facts.note: Requirement confirmed; subsection number differs between the 2021 and 2024 editions.

facts.fact: Where a dryer exhaust duct passes within 1-1/4 inches of the face of framing members, steel shield plates at least 0.062 inch thick must protect it, extending at least 2 inches above sole plates and below top plates.
facts.note: Requirement confirmed; subsection number differs between editions.
facts.reviewed: The code states shield plates of 0.062-inch steel. No. 16 gage (0.0598 in) is slightly thinner, so 'at least No. 16 gage' understates the requirement.

facts.source: IMC 2021 504.2; Sec. 504 (dryer exhaust duct power ventilators)
facts.fact: Fire dampers and combination fire/smoke dampers are not allowed in clothes dryer exhaust ducts, and booster fans are not allowed unless they are listed dryer exhaust duct power ventilators (UL 705).
facts.reviewed: IMC 504.5 is dryer makeup air, not dampers or booster fans. The damper prohibition is in 504.2, and dryer exhaust duct power ventilators (DEPV) are covered by the separate DEPV provisions of Sec. 504.

facts.fact: IMC 505.2: a domestic kitchen exhaust hood able to exhaust more than 400 cfm must have makeup air at about the same rate, with a means of closure, automatically controlled to run with the hood. IRC M1503.6: makeup air (at about the exhaust rate, through an automatically opening gravity or electrically operated damper) is required for exhaust systems over 400 cfm only where a fuel-burning appliance that is neither direct-vent nor mechanical-draft is located inside the dwelling unit's air barrier.
facts.reviewed: This mixes the IMC and IRC rules. Under the IRC (M1503.6), makeup air for hoods over 400 cfm is required only where a fuel-burning appliance that is neither direct-vent nor mechanical-draft is inside the dwelling's air barrier. An exam is likely to test that condition.

facts.fact: Ducts serving domestic kitchen cooking appliances must be galvanized steel, stainless steel or copper, have smooth interior surfaces, be airtight, have a backdraft damper, and discharge outdoors (not into an attic or crawl space). Exceptions: Schedule 40 PVC is allowed for downdraft exhaust ducts installed under a concrete slab on grade (with other conditions), and listed and labeled ductless range hoods need not discharge outdoors where other ventilation is provided.
facts.reviewed: States the rule as absolute and leaves out exceptions an exam would test: Schedule 40 PVC is allowed for downdraft systems under a slab on grade, and listed ductless range hoods need not discharge outdoors.

facts.fact: A Type I hood is required over commercial cooking appliances that produce grease or smoke (medium-, heavy- and extra-heavy-duty appliances), and the Type I hood must have an automatic fire suppression system.
A Type II hood is a general kitchen hood for appliances that produce heat, steam, odors or products of combustion but not grease or smoke, such as dishwashers and some ovens.
Commercial cooking appliances required to have a Type I hood must also have an approved automatic fire suppression system meeting the IBC and IFC.

A canopy-type commercial kitchen hood must overhang the top horizontal surface of the appliances by at least 6 inches on all open sides, and the front lower lip may be no more than 4 ft above the cooking surface.
Type I hoods must be built of steel at least 0.0466 inch (No. 18 gage) or stainless steel at least 0.0335 inch (No. 20 gage).
Grease ducts serving Type I hoods must be steel at least 0.055 inch (No. 16 gage) thick or stainless steel at least 0.044 inch (No. 18 gage) thick.

Horizontal grease ducts must slope toward the hood or an approved grease reservoir at least 1/4 inch per foot (2 percent); horizontal runs longer than 75 ft must slope at least 1 inch per foot (8.3 percent).
Grease duct systems serving Type I hoods must maintain an air velocity of at least 500 feet per minute.

Where a grease duct enclosure is not required, the grease duct must have at least 18 inches of clearance to combustible construction and 3 inches to noncombustible construction, unless a listed clearance-reduction method is used.

The lowest edge of grease filters must be at least 0.5 ft above cooking surfaces with no exposed flame, 2 ft above exposed flame and burners, and 3.5 ft above exposed charcoal and charbroil-type fires.
Grease filters must be installed at an angle of at least 45 degrees from horizontal and be equipped with a drip tray beneath their lower edge.

Rooftop grease duct exhaust outlets must discharge at least 40 inches above the roof surface, at least 10 ft horizontally from adjacent buildings, property lines and air intake openings, and at least 10 ft above grade.

Commercial kitchen makeup air must be supplied at approximately the same rate as the exhaust, and in general the makeup air temperature may not differ from the kitchen air temperature by more than 10 degrees F.
Unlisted wall-mounted canopy hoods are commonly required to exhaust 200 cfm per linear foot for light-duty, 300 for medium-duty, 400 for heavy-duty and 550 for extra-heavy-duty appliances.
facts.note: Recalled table values; not confirmed for the 2021 edition, and listed hoods (UL 710) use their listed rates.

facts.fact: Flexible air ducts must be tested and classified per UL 181 as Class 0 or Class 1.
The IMC does not limit the length of flexible air ducts (as opposed to flexible air connectors).
Flexible air connectors are limited to 14 ft in length and may not pass through any wall, floor or ceiling.
Flexible air ducts and flexible air connectors may not be used where the air temperature exceeds 250 degrees F.
Gypsum board may be used to form air shafts only for return air, where the air temperature does not exceed 125 degrees F and the gypsum surface stays above the airstream dew point.

Duct joints and seams must be sealed; tapes and mastics must be listed to UL 181A (rigid fiberglass duct, marked 181A-P, 181A-M or 181A-H) or UL 181B (flex duct, marked 181B-FX or 181B-M). Ordinary unlisted cloth duct tape is not acceptable.

facts.source: ADC Flexible Duct Performance & Installation Standards
facts.fact: Industry installation standards call for flexible duct to be supported at intervals of no more than 5 ft, with sag between supports no more than 1/2 inch per foot of spacing, and the duct fully extended without kinks.
facts.note: Industry standard (Air Diffusion Council); code defers to manufacturer instructions.

facts.fact: Duct coverings and linings, including adhesives, must have a flame spread index of no more than 25 and a smoke-developed index of no more than 50 when tested to ASTM E84 / UL 723.

External duct insulation and factory-insulated flexible duct must be printed at intervals of no more than 10 ft with the manufacturer's name, installed R-value, and flame spread and smoke-developed indexes.

Materials exposed inside a plenum generally must be noncombustible or have a flame spread index of no more than 25 and a smoke-developed index of no more than 50; electrical cable in plenums must be plenum-rated per NFPA 70.

Stud wall cavities and spaces between solid floor joists used as plenums may carry return air only (never supply air), may not be part of a fire-resistance-rated assembly, and stud cavities may not convey air from more than one floor level.

Smoke detectors are required in the return air duct or plenum of air distribution systems with a design capacity greater than 2,000 cfm, located upstream of filters, exhaust connections and outdoor air connections. Exception: they are not required where all portions of the building served by the system are protected by area smoke detectors connected to a fire alarm system per the IFC.
facts.reviewed: Leaves out the common exception: return-air duct detectors are not required where all areas served are covered by area smoke detection connected to a fire alarm system.

facts.fact: Return air risers serving two or more stories in a return system larger than 15,000 cfm need a smoke detector at each story, upstream of the connection to the common riser.
When a required duct smoke detector activates, it must shut down the air distribution system it serves.
Fire dampers must have a 1-1/2-hour rating in assemblies rated less than 3 hours, and a 3-hour rating in assemblies rated 3 hours or more.
Smoke dampers must have a leakage rating of at least Class II and an elevated temperature rating of at least 250 degrees F.

Fire and smoke dampers need an access opening large enough to inspect and maintain them, and each access point must be labeled on the outside with letters at least 1/2 inch high reading FIRE DAMPER, SMOKE DAMPER or FIRE/SMOKE DAMPER.
A fire damper is not required where steel exhaust subducts extend at least 22 inches vertically inside an exhaust shaft and the exhaust fan runs continuously to maintain upward airflow.

Under the 2021 IECC, residential supply and return ducts located outside conditioned space must be insulated to at least R-8 if 3 inches in diameter or larger, and at least R-6 if smaller than 3 inches.
facts.note: Edition-dependent: the 2018 IECC allowed R-6/R-4.2 for ducts outside attics; 2021 applies R-8/R-6 to all ducts outside conditioned space.

facts.fact: Residential ducts, air handlers and filter boxes must be sealed, and building framing cavities may not be used as ducts or plenums.
Residential duct leakage testing is done at a pressure of 25 Pascals (0.1 inch w.c.).

Total residential duct leakage may not exceed 4.0 cfm per 100 sq ft of conditioned floor area (rough-in with air handler, or post-construction), 3.0 cfm per 100 sq ft at rough-in without the air handler, or 8.0 cfm per 100 sq ft when all ducts and the air handler are inside the thermal envelope.
Worked example: a 2,000 sq ft house tested post-construction may have at most 2,000 / 100 x 4.0 = 80 cfm of total duct leakage at 25 Pa.
Residential mechanical system piping carrying fluids above 105 degrees F or below 55 degrees F must be insulated to at least R-3.
A heat pump with supplementary electric resistance heat must have controls that keep the resistance heat off when the heat pump compressor can meet the load, except during defrost.

The thermostat for a dwelling's primary heating or cooling system must be programmable by time and day, and is initially set by the manufacturer to no higher than 70 degrees F for heating and no lower than 78 degrees F for cooling.
facts.note: Programmable-thermostat requirement confirmed for 2021; the 70/78 initial set points are from prior editions and were not re-confirmed.

facts.fact: Residential duct leakage testing must follow ANSI/RESNET/ICC 380 or ASTM E1554 and may be done either at rough-in or post-construction.
Combustion air for gas-fired appliances is governed by the IFGC (Section 304); for oil-fired appliances the IMC refers to NFPA 31.

Direct-vent appliances, gas appliances other than Category I (natural draft) type, and appliances with power burners take combustion air as specified in the manufacturer's installation instructions rather than the room-volume and opening rules.
facts.reviewed: This rule is in the main text of 304.1, not an exception. The only 304.1 exception covers Type 1 clothes dryers.

facts.fact: Under the standard method, indoor combustion air is adequate when the room (plus spaces connected by proper openings) has at least 50 cubic feet of volume for each 1,000 Btu/h of total appliance input.
Worked example: a 100,000 Btu/h furnace and a 40,000 Btu/h water heater in the same space total 140,000 Btu/h, so the space needs at least 140 x 50 = 7,000 cubic feet to use indoor air alone.

The known air infiltration rate method must be used instead of the 50 cu ft rule when the building's air infiltration rate is known to be less than 0.40 air changes per hour; its formulas use 21 cu ft/ACH per 1,000 Btu/h for non-fan-assisted appliances and 15 cu ft/ACH per 1,000 Btu/h for fan-assisted appliances.

Openings combining indoor spaces on the same story must each have at least 1 square inch of free area per 1,000 Btu/h of total input, but not less than 100 square inches each; one opening starts within 12 inches of the top and one within 12 inches of the bottom, and the minimum dimension is 3 inches.

Worked example: combining rooms for a 140,000 Btu/h total input requires two openings of 140 square inches each (1 sq in per 1,000 Btu/h); a 60,000 Btu/h input would still need the 100 sq in minimum for each opening.
Openings that combine indoor spaces on different stories must have a total free area of at least 2 square inches per 1,000 Btu/h of total input.
