With two permanent openings to the outdoors (one within 12 in of the top, one within 12 in of the bottom), each opening needs 1 sq in per 4,000 Btu/h if it connects directly outdoors or through vertical ducts, or 1 sq in per 2,000 Btu/h if it uses horizontal ducts.

Worked example: a 120,000 Btu/h appliance using two outdoor openings through vertical ducts needs 120,000 / 4,000 = 30 sq in per opening; through horizontal ducts it needs 120,000 / 2,000 = 60 sq in per opening.

A single permanent outdoor opening must start within 12 inches of the top of the space, have at least 1 sq in per 3,000 Btu/h of total input, be no smaller than the combined area of all vent connectors in the space, and the appliances need at least 1 inch clearance at sides and back and 6 inches at the front.
Mechanical combustion air must supply at least 0.35 cfm per 1,000 Btu/h of total appliance input, and each appliance must be interlocked so it cannot operate unless the combustion air fan is running.

When the design and free area of louvers and grilles are unknown, assume wood louvers have 25 percent free area and metal louvers have 75 percent; motorized louvers must be interlocked with the appliance.

Worked example: if 100 sq in of free area is required and metal louvers (75 percent free area) are used, the louver's gross size must be at least 100 / 0.75 = about 133 sq in; with wood louvers it would be 100 / 0.25 = 400 sq in.

Combustion air ducts must have a cross-sectional area at least equal to the required free area of the openings they serve, a minimum dimension of 3 inches, and separate ducts for the upper and lower openings.
Where exhaust fans, clothes dryers or kitchen ventilation could interfere with appliance operation (for example, by causing backdrafting), makeup air must be provided.

Category I appliances operate with nonpositive vent static pressure and a flue gas temperature that avoids excessive condensate in the vent; Category II also has nonpositive pressure but produces condensate.

Category III appliances operate with positive vent pressure without excessive condensate; Category IV appliances operate with positive vent pressure and produce condensate (typical 90-percent-plus condensing furnaces).

Category I and draft-hood appliances may vent through Type B gas vent, a chimney, or single-wall metal pipe as allowed; listed vented wall furnaces use Type B-W vent; Category II, III and IV appliances use the vent system specified by the manufacturer.
Plastic pipe (PVC, CPVC, polypropylene) may be used for venting only where the appliance manufacturer's listed instructions call for it, as with Category IV condensing appliances.
Type B gas vents (double-wall, for Category I gas appliances) are listed to UL 441, while Type L vents (for oil appliances and gas appliances listed for them) are listed to UL 641.
Vent connectors must have no dips or sags and must rise toward the vent or chimney at a slope of at least 1/4 inch per foot.

The maximum horizontal length of a single-wall vent connector is 75 percent of the height of the chimney or vent; for a Type B double-wall connector it is 100 percent of the vent height (except engineered systems).
Worked example: with a 20 ft high Type B vent, a single-wall connector may run horizontally no more than 0.75 x 20 = 15 ft, while a Type B double-wall connector could run 20 ft.

When sizing common vent systems with the IFGC tables, the maximum vent connector horizontal length is 18 inches (1.5 ft) per inch of connector diameter; for example, a 4-inch connector may run 6 ft and a 6-inch connector 9 ft.
When two or more connectors enter a common vent or chimney, the smaller connector must enter at the highest level that headroom and clearances allow.

A single-wall metal vent connector serving a listed appliance with a draft hood (or listed for Type B vent) needs at least 6 inches of clearance to combustible material, unless the listing specifies otherwise.

Single-wall metal vent connectors may not be used in attics or crawl spaces, and may be used in other unconditioned spaces only where the 99 percent winter design temperature is 5 degrees F or higher.
A vent connector entering a masonry chimney must enter at least 12 inches above the lowest portion of the interior of the chimney flue and may not extend past the inner face of the chimney liner.
facts.note: Could not confirm a 12-inch-above-flue-bottom entry rule in IFGC 503.10. The code text says the connector must enter above the extreme bottom of the chimney to avoid stoppage and must not extend so far that it restricts the flue.
facts.reviewed: Could not confirm a 12-inch-above-flue-bottom entry rule in IFGC 503.10. The code text says the connector must enter above the extreme bottom of the chimney to avoid stoppage and must not extend so far that it restricts the flue.

facts.fact: A chimney for residential-type or low-heat appliances must extend at least 3 ft above the highest point where it passes through the roof and at least 2 ft higher than any part of the building within 10 ft horizontally.
facts.reviewed: The 3-2-10 rule in 503.5.4 applies to chimneys for residential-type or low-heat appliances. Medium- and high-heat appliance chimneys need more height.

facts.fact: Gas vents larger than 12 inches, or located less than 8 ft from a vertical wall, must terminate at least 2 ft above the highest point where they pass through the roof and at least 2 ft above any part of the building within 10 ft horizontally.

A listed Type B gas vent 12 inches or smaller with a listed cap, at least 8 ft from a vertical wall, terminates by roof pitch: flat to 6/12 needs 1 ft minimum height above the roof, over 6/12 to 7/12 needs 1.25 ft, and over 11/12 to 12/12 needs 4 ft.

A Type B or L gas vent must terminate at least 5 ft in vertical height above the highest connected appliance draft hood or flue collar, and a Type B-W vent at least 12 ft above the bottom of the wall furnace.

A mechanical draft (power vent) terminal must be at least 4 ft below, 4 ft horizontally from, or 1 ft above any door, operable window or gravity air inlet, and at least 3 ft above any forced-air inlet within 10 ft.
Mechanical draft vent terminals must be at least 12 inches above finished grade and at least 7 ft above grade where located next to public walkways.
facts.note: The 12-inch-above-grade rule is in IFGC 503.8. The 7-ft public-walkway rule comes from NFPA 54, and I could not confirm it in the 2021 IFGC text.
facts.reviewed: The 12-inch-above-grade rule is in IFGC 503.8. The 7-ft public-walkway rule comes from NFPA 54, and I could not confirm it in the 2021 IFGC text.

facts.fact: Direct-vent terminals must be at least 6 inches from any air opening into the building for inputs of 10,000 Btu/h or less, 9 inches for over 10,000 to 50,000 Btu/h, and 12 inches for over 50,000 Btu/h, with the terminal and intake at least 12 inches above grade.

When an appliance is permanently disconnected from an existing chimney or vent (for example, a furnace replaced by a separately vented condensing furnace), the remaining chimney or vent must be resized as needed so the remaining appliance gets proper draft and condensation is controlled.

In the longest length method of sizing gas piping, the length from the point of delivery (meter or regulator) to the most remote outlet is used to select pipe size for every section, using each section's own load.
The common low-pressure natural gas sizing table for Schedule 40 steel pipe is based on inlet pressure under 2 psi, a 0.5 inch water column pressure drop, and gas specific gravity of 0.60.
IFGC natural gas tables give capacity in cubic feet per hour (CFH); undiluted propane tables give capacity in thousands of Btu per hour, based on a specific gravity of 1.50.

To convert appliance input to gas flow, divide Btu/h by the gas heating value; with natural gas at about 1,000 Btu per cubic foot, a 100,000 Btu/h furnace needs about 100 CFH, and with propane at about 2,500 Btu per cubic foot it needs about 40 CFH.
facts.note: Use the actual heating value from the gas supplier when known.

facts.fact: Natural gas (specific gravity about 0.60) is lighter than air and rises, while propane (specific gravity about 1.5) is heavier than air and collects in low spots such as basements and pits.
Propane contains about 91,500 Btu per gallon (about 2,500 Btu per cubic foot of vapor), natural gas about 1,000 to 1,050 Btu per cubic foot, and one therm equals 100,000 Btu.
Typical gas furnace manifold pressure is about 3.5 inches w.c. for natural gas and about 10 inches w.c. for propane; always set to the appliance rating plate and manufacturer's instructions.
facts.note: Typical values; the rating plate governs.

facts.fact: Natural gas piping inside buildings is limited to 5 psig operating pressure unless specific conditions are met, such as all-welded or brazed joints or piping in a ventilated chase.
Gas piping must be pressure-tested at no less than 1-1/2 times the proposed maximum working pressure, but never less than 3 psig, regardless of design pressure.
The gas piping pressure test must last at least 10 minutes.
Gas piping may be tested with air, nitrogen, carbon dioxide or an inert gas; oxygen may never be used as a test medium.
Mechanical gauges used for gas piping tests must have a range whose highest scale value is no more than five times the test pressure, so a small pressure loss is readable.

During a gas pressure test, appliances rated for less than the test pressure must be disconnected and the outlets capped; appliances rated for at least the test pressure may be isolated by closing their shutoff valves.
Leak checks with matches, candles, open flames or any other ignition source are prohibited; use a leak-detection solution or approved gas detector.
Each appliance needs an accessible shutoff valve in the same room, located within 6 ft of the appliance and upstream of the union, connector or quick-disconnect serving it.
Gas shutoff valves may not be located in concealed locations or inside furnace plenums.

A flexible appliance connector may be no longer than 6 ft overall, only one connector may be used per appliance, and connectors may not be concealed in or passed through walls, floors, partitions, ceilings or appliance housings (limited exceptions apply).

Where a sediment trap is not built into the appliance, one must be installed downstream of the appliance shutoff valve as close to the appliance inlet as practical, made from a tee with a capped nipple in the bottom outlet; illuminating appliances, ranges, clothes dryers, decorative vented appliances and outdoor grills are exempt.

CSST gas piping systems must be bonded to the electrical service grounding electrode system with a bonding jumper no smaller than 6 AWG copper (or equivalent), no longer than 75 ft, attached to a metallic pipe, fitting or CSST fitting.
facts.note: Section is 310.1.1 in 2021; renumbered 310.2 in 2024.

facts.fact: Underground gas piping must be at least 12 inches below grade; individual lines to outside lights, grills or similar outdoor appliances may be 8 inches deep where approved and not subject to physical damage.

Gas piping installed through holes or notches in framing less than 1-1/2 inches from the face of the member must be protected by steel shield plates at least 0.0575 inch (No. 16 gage) thick, extending at least 4 inches beyond the member (above sole plates, below top plates, each side of studs).
Above-ground outdoor gas piping must be elevated at least 3-1/2 inches above the ground, and at least 3-1/2 inches above roof surfaces where run across a roof.
Plastic (PE) gas pipe may be installed outdoors underground only, and must have a yellow insulated copper tracer wire no smaller than 18 AWG (or other approved locating means).
Gas piping may not be installed in or through ducts, clothes chutes, chimneys or gas vents, dumbwaiters or elevator shafts.

Horizontal steel gas pipe supports are spaced at most 6 ft for 1/2 inch pipe, 8 ft for 3/4 and 1 inch pipe, and 10 ft for 1-1/4 inch and larger; vertical 1-1/4 inch and larger is supported at every floor level.
Horizontal smooth-wall tubing (such as copper) used for gas is supported every 4 ft for 1/2 inch, 6 ft for 5/8 and 3/4 inch, and 8 ft for 7/8 and 1 inch; CSST is supported per the manufacturer.
Exposed gas piping other than steel pipe must be labeled with yellow labels reading 'Gas' in black letters at intervals of no more than 5 ft, except in the same room as the appliance served.
Gas pressure regulators that need a vent must have the vent piped to the outdoors, unless the regulator has a listed vent-limiting device.
Hydronic piping (other than ground-source loops) must be hydrostatically tested at 1-1/2 times the maximum system design pressure, but not less than 100 psi, for at least 15 minutes.
Ground-source heat pump loop piping must be pressure tested with water at 100 psi for 15 minutes with no observed leaks before trenches are backfilled.
facts.note: Confirmed for the 2024 IMC (1210.10); not confirmed for the 2021 edition.

facts.fact: Steam and hot water boilers must be protected by a low-water cutoff control; coil-type and water-tube boilers that require forced circulation may instead use a flow-sensing control.

Steam and hot water boilers must have a safety or relief valve; the discharge pipe must be the same size as the valve outlet, and no shutoff valve may be installed between the relief valve and the boiler or in the discharge line.

Clearances around boilers must follow the manufacturer's installation instructions; where none are given, passageways around all sides of a boiler must be at least 18 inches wide unless otherwise approved, to allow inspection, maintenance and repair.
facts.reviewed: States the 18-inch rule as absolute. The manufacturer's installation instructions govern boiler clearances first, and 18 inches applies only where they do not specify.

facts.fact: ASME Section IV heating boilers are low-pressure boilers: steam boilers operating at no more than 15 psi and hot water boilers at no more than 160 psi and 250 degrees F.
A typical residential hot water boiler is fitted with a 30 psi relief valve, and a relief valve may never be set above the boiler's maximum allowable working pressure.
facts.note: Typical residential value.

facts.fact: A column of water exerts 0.433 psi per foot of height (2.31 ft of water per psi). Example: to lift water to the top of a system 25 ft above the fill valve takes about 25 x 0.433 = 10.8 psi, plus a few psi of extra pressure at the top to vent air.

facts.source: Q = 500 x GPM x delta T
facts.fact: Hydronic heat transfer: Btu/h = 500 x GPM x temperature difference (degrees F), where 500 = 8.33 lb/gal x 60 min/h x 1 Btu/lb-F. Example: 10 GPM with a 20 F drop carries 500 x 10 x 20 = 100,000 Btu/h.

facts.source: Q = 500 x GPM x delta T
facts.fact: Rearranged: GPM = Btu/h / (500 x delta T). Example: a 60,000 Btu/h zone designed for a 20 F temperature drop needs 60,000 / (500 x 20) = 6 GPM.

In a closed hydronic system the expansion tank connection is the point of no pressure change, so circulators are normally placed to pump away from the expansion tank, raising rather than lowering system pressure.
Hot water boilers and closed hydronic systems must have an expansion tank to absorb the change in water volume as the water heats, preventing the relief valve from opening during normal operation.

Refrigerant safety groups use a letter for toxicity (A = lower toxicity, B = higher toxicity) and a number for flammability (1 = no flame propagation, 2L = lower flammability, 2 = flammable, 3 = higher flammability).
Class 2L (mildly flammable) refrigerants are class 2 refrigerants with a maximum burning velocity of no more than 10 cm/s.
Common safety classifications: R-22, R-410A, R-134a and R-404A are A1; R-32, R-454B and R-1234yf are A2L; R-290 (propane) and R-600a (isobutane) are A3; R-123 is B1; R-717 (ammonia) is B2L.
Refrigerants in the 400 series (such as R-410A, R-407C, R-404A) are zeotropic blends, and 500-series refrigerants (such as R-502) are azeotropic blends that behave like a single substance.
Zeotropic blends should be charged as a liquid (throttled into the suction side so liquid does not reach the compressor) because charging as vapor can change the blend's composition (fractionation).

Blends with temperature glide (such as R-407C) boil over a range of temperatures at one pressure; use the dew point temperature to calculate superheat and the bubble point temperature to calculate subcooling.

facts.source: IPCC AR4 GWP values (used by EPA)
facts.fact: Approximate 100-year global warming potentials: R-410A about 2,088, R-32 about 675, and R-454B about 466, which is why R-32 and R-454B qualify as replacements under a 700 GWP limit.

Under EPA's Technology Transitions rule, new residential and light commercial air conditioning and heat pump systems manufactured or imported on or after January 1, 2025 must use a refrigerant with a GWP below 700 (in practice, A2L refrigerants such as R-454B or R-32 instead of R-410A).
facts.note: Dated rule; amended May 2026.

facts.fact: A final rule published May 26, 2026 removed the installation deadline (originally January 1, 2026) for residential and light commercial AC and heat pump systems with GWP of 700 or more that were manufactured or imported before January 1, 2025, so remaining legacy R-410A systems may still be installed.
facts.note: As reported by Holland & Knight, May 2026; check for later changes.
facts.reviewed: This is a recent regulatory change that rests on one law-firm summary. I could not confirm the May 26, 2026 rule or its exact scope against EPA or the Federal Register.

facts.fact: Refrigeration system components must be located outdoors or in a machinery room when the refrigerant quantity in any single independent circuit exceeds the amount allowed by IMC Table 1103.1 for the space.

The allowable refrigerant charge for an occupied space is the table limit (pounds per 1,000 cubic feet) times the room volume divided by 1,000. Example: R-410A at 26 lb per 1,000 cu ft in a 20 x 20 x 10 ft (4,000 cu ft) room allows 26 x 4,000 / 1,000 = 104 lb.
facts.note: Calculation method confirmed; the R-410A table value (26 lb/1,000 cu ft) was confirmed only from a 2024-edition study source.

facts.fact: Machinery room emergency ventilation must be at least Q = 100 x the square root of G (in cfm), where G is pounds of refrigerant in the largest system. Example: a 100 lb system needs 100 x 10 = 1,000 cfm.
Normal ventilation of an occupied refrigeration machinery room must be at least the greater of 0.5 cfm per square foot of room area or 20 cfm per person.
Refrigeration machinery rooms must have a refrigerant detector that activates an alarm and mechanical ventilation at a concentration no higher than the refrigerant's occupational exposure limit.
Refrigerant circuit access ports located outdoors must have locking, tamper-resistant caps or be otherwise secured to prevent unauthorized access (for example, refrigerant huffing).
Refrigerant piping may not be installed in exit stairways, stair landings, means of egress, or elevator, dumbwaiter or other shafts containing moving objects.
Field-erected refrigerant piping must be pressure tested before operation using dry nitrogen or another inert gas; oxygen, air, combustible gases and mixtures containing them may not be used.

Many A2L split systems (R-454B, R-32) are required by their UL 60335-2-40 listing to include a refrigerant leak detection system that, when it senses a leak, runs the indoor blower to dilute the refrigerant and disables the compressor and other potential ignition sources.
facts.note: Requirement depends on charge size and equipment type; follow the listing and manufacturer instructions.

facts.fact: Flowing low-pressure dry nitrogen through copper refrigerant lines while brazing prevents copper oxide scale from forming inside the pipe, which could otherwise clog metering devices and filters.

Systems are evacuated with a vacuum pump to remove air, non-condensables and moisture; a common target is 500 microns or lower, measured with a micron gauge, followed by a decay (standing) test to check for leaks or remaining moisture.
facts.note: Manufacturer instructions may set different targets.

facts.fact: Gauge pressure (psig) plus atmospheric pressure (about 14.7 psi at sea level) equals absolute pressure (psia); atmospheric pressure equals 29.92 inches of mercury, or 760,000 microns.
One micron is 1/1,000 of a millimeter of mercury; one inch of mercury equals 25,400 microns, and one psi equals about 2.04 inches of mercury or 27.7 inches of water column.

Since April 10, 2020, EPA's Section 608 leak repair rules apply only to appliances with a full charge of 50 pounds or more of an ozone-depleting (CFC or HCFC) refrigerant, such as R-22; appliances containing only HFC substitutes are excluded from 82.157.
facts.note: HFC leak repair is now covered separately under 40 CFR 84 (see ER&R facts).

facts.fact: Leak rate thresholds that trigger repair: 20 percent per year for commercial refrigeration, 30 percent for industrial process refrigeration, and 10 percent for comfort cooling and other appliances with 50 lb or more.

Once an appliance exceeds its leak rate threshold, leaks must be repaired within 30 days of the refrigerant addition that revealed the exceedance, or 120 days if an industrial process shutdown is needed.

After a leak repair, an initial verification test is required (within the 30- or 120-day repair window), and a follow-up verification test within 10 days of the successful initial test or of the system returning to normal operating conditions.

If an owner chooses to retrofit or retire a leaking appliance instead of repairing it, a retrofit or retirement plan must be developed within 30 days, and the work generally completed within one year of the plan's date.
An appliance with 50 lb or more that leaks 125 percent or more of its full charge in one calendar year must be reported to EPA by March 1 of the following year.

After a leak exceeds the threshold, periodic leak inspections are required: quarterly for commercial or industrial process refrigeration with 500 lb or more (until four consecutive quarters are below threshold), and annually for those with 50 to under 500 lb and for comfort cooling.

Annualizing leak rate = (pounds added / pounds full charge) x (365 / days since refrigerant was last added) x 100. Example: adding 10 lb to a 100 lb system 73 days after the last addition gives 10/100 x 365/73 x 100 = 50 percent per year.

For appliances with 50 lb or more of ODS refrigerant, the leak rate must be calculated every time refrigerant is added (unless the addition follows a retrofit or installation, or is a seasonal variance).
Leak repair records (inspections, verification tests, refrigerant additions) must be kept for at least three years; full-charge records are kept until three years after the appliance is retired.

Starting January 1, 2026, EPA's HFC Emissions Reduction and Reclamation rule extends leak repair to appliances with 15 lb or more of an HFC or substitute refrigerant with GWP above 53, using the same 20 / 30 / 10 percent thresholds; residential and light commercial AC and heat pumps are excluded.
facts.note: Dated rule; EPA has said it may reconsider parts of the leak program (proposed TRU exemption May 2026).

facts.fact: Automatic leak detection is required for new commercial refrigeration and industrial process refrigeration systems with 1,500 lb or more of HFC (GWP above 53) installed on or after January 1, 2026, and by January 1, 2027 for such systems installed from 2017 through 2025.

From January 1, 2026, reclaimed HFC refrigerant may contain no more than 15 percent virgin HFC by weight; from January 1, 2029, supermarket systems, refrigerated transport and automatic commercial ice makers must be serviced with reclaimed HFCs.

Starting January 1, 2028, disposable refrigerant cylinders must be sent to a reclaimer, recycler, final processor or supplier to remove the heel, or a certified technician must evacuate the cylinder to 15 inches of mercury vacuum and give a certification statement to the final processor.

Before opening or disposing of a high-pressure appliance (such as R-22 or R-410A) with less than 200 lb of charge, refrigerant must be recovered to 0 inches of mercury vacuum (0 psig), regardless of when the recovery equipment was made.
High-pressure appliances with 200 lb or more must be evacuated to 10 inches of mercury vacuum using recovery equipment made on or after November 15, 1993 (4 inches with older equipment).

Medium-pressure appliances (such as R-134a or R-12) must be evacuated to 10 inches of mercury vacuum if under 200 lb, or 15 inches if 200 lb or more, using equipment made on or after November 15, 1993 (4 inches for either with older equipment).

Low-pressure appliances (such as R-123 or R-11 centrifugal chillers) must be evacuated to 25 mm of mercury absolute using recovery equipment made on or after November 15, 1993 (25 inches of mercury vacuum with older equipment); very high-pressure appliances (such as R-23 or R-503) must be evacuated to 0 inches of mercury.
facts.reviewed: Leaves out the date split in Table 1. Low-pressure appliances require 25 mm Hg absolute only with recovery equipment made on or after November 15, 1993; older equipment requires 25 inches of mercury vacuum.

facts.fact: For small appliances, recovery equipment made on or after November 15, 1993 must recover 90 percent of the refrigerant if the compressor runs or 80 percent if it does not; alternatively, the appliance may be evacuated to 4 inches of mercury vacuum.

For non-major repairs not followed by an evacuation to atmosphere, medium-, high- and very high-pressure appliances may be evacuated to just 0 psig before opening, and low-pressure appliances pressurized to 0 psig.
A major repair is one that removes the compressor, condenser, evaporator or auxiliary heat exchange coil, or that uncovers more than 4 square inches of refrigerant flow area for more than 15 minutes.

If leaks make the required evacuation level impossible, isolate the leaking parts, evacuate the non-leaking parts to the normal level, and evacuate leaking parts to the lowest level attainable without contaminating the refrigerant, which may not be above 0 psig.

System-dependent (passive) recovery equipment, which relies on the appliance's own compressor or pressure, may not be used on appliances with a full charge of more than 15 lb, unless it is a permanently attached pump-out unit.

Recovery and recycling equipment must be certified by an EPA-approved testing organization (to AHRI 740 for equipment made since January 1, 2017), labeled as certified, and equipped with low-loss fittings on all hoses.

EPA defines appliance pressure classes by liquid saturation pressure at 104 degrees F: high-pressure is 170 to 355 psia (R-22, R-410A, R-407C, R-502); medium-pressure is 45 to 170 psia (R-12, R-134a, R-500).

Low-pressure appliances have a saturation pressure below 45 psia at 104 degrees F (R-11, R-113, R-123, R-245fa); very high-pressure appliances have a critical temperature below 104 F or pressure above 355 psia (R-13, R-23, R-503).

Type II certification covers servicing and disposal of medium-, high- and very high-pressure appliances (except small appliances and motor vehicle AC); Universal certification covers Types I, II and III.
Each EPA 608 exam has at least 25 Core questions plus 25 questions per technician type; a Universal test is 100 questions (25 Core + 25 each for Types I, II and III).
The passing score for closed-book EPA 608 tests (Type I, II, III and Universal) is 70 percent; Type I tests given in a mail-in format require 84 percent.
Type II, Type III and Universal EPA 608 tests must be closed-book and proctored, with at least one proctor for every 50 test takers; only Type I may be offered in an unproctored mail-in format.
EPA Section 608 technician certification does not expire; EPA has reserved the right to require recertification in the future but has not done so.
Certified technicians must keep a copy of their certificate at their place of business, and keep it for three years after they stop working as technicians.

Since January 1, 2018 the refrigerant sales restriction covers non-exempt substitutes (such as HFCs) as well as CFCs and HCFCs; buyers must be EPA-certified technicians or employ one and give the seller proof.

Small cans of non-exempt substitute refrigerant for motor vehicle AC (2 lb or less) may be sold to the public if they have a unique fitting and, for cans made since January 1, 2018, a self-sealing valve.
Refrigerant sellers must keep invoices showing the buyer's name, sale date and quantity for three years.

Used refrigerant may be sold to a new owner for use as a refrigerant only after it has been reclaimed by an EPA-certified reclaimer (limited exceptions include MVAC recycling and transfers within the same company).

Certified reclaimers must reprocess refrigerant to the purity specifications of 40 CFR 82 Appendix A (based on AHRI Standard 700), verify each batch by laboratory analysis, release no more than 1.5 percent of refrigerant during reclamation, and report to EPA annually by February 1.

Recover means removing refrigerant in any condition and storing it in an external container without testing or processing it; recycle means cleaning it for reuse (typically by oil separation and filter driers) without meeting full specifications; reclaim means reprocessing it to Appendix A (AHRI 700) purity verified by analysis.

The venting prohibition does not apply to certain exempt substitutes: carbon dioxide, nitrogen and water in any application; ammonia in commercial or industrial process refrigeration and absorption units; and hydrocarbons such as propane and isobutane only in specified end uses.

De minimis refrigerant releases made during good-faith attempts to recover, recycle or properly dispose of refrigerant (while following required practices and using certified equipment) are not violations of the venting prohibition.

Nitrogen mixed with a trace of refrigerant used as a holding charge or leak-test gas may be released, but a technician may not add nitrogen to a charged system to avoid recovery; the system must first be evacuated to the required level.

The Clean Air Act authorizes EPA to pay an award of up to $10,000 to a person who provides information leading to a criminal conviction or civil penalty for violating the Act, including illegal venting.

The final processor in the disposal chain (such as a scrap recycler or landfill) for small appliances, MVACs and MVAC-like appliances must either recover remaining refrigerant itself or obtain a signed statement giving the name and address of the person who recovered it and the date of recovery.
Final processors must keep the signed recovery statements or contracts for three years.

Since January 1, 2018, technicians who recover refrigerant from appliances with more than 5 and less than 50 lb for disposal must keep records for three years, including company name, location, date, refrigerant type and monthly quantities recovered.
Refillable refrigerant recovery cylinders are painted gray with a yellow top (shoulder) and must be DOT-approved for recovered refrigerant.

Refillable recovery cylinders (DOT 4BA or 4BW) must be hydrostatically retested (requalified) every 5 years, and the most recent test date is stamped on the cylinder; an out-of-date cylinder may not be refilled.
facts.note: 5-year interval is the general DOT rule taught in EPA 608 training; DOT allows longer intervals only in certain exclusive-service cases.

facts.fact: Disposable (DOT 39) refrigerant cylinders may never be refilled or used to hold recovered refrigerant.

Since January 2020, AHRI Guideline N calls for all new refrigerant containers to be one color (RAL 7044 light gray) instead of color-coded by refrigerant; the label identifies the refrigerant, and flammable refrigerants (such as A2L and A3) also carry a red band on the shoulder or top.
Refrigerant cylinders should never be heated with an open flame or exposed to temperatures above 125 degrees F; heat raises internal pressure and liquid expansion can rupture an overfilled cylinder.
facts.note: Common manufacturer and training limit.

facts.fact: Different refrigerants must not be mixed in one recovery cylinder, because mixed refrigerant generally cannot be reclaimed and may have to be destroyed.

Recovering liquid first (for example, with the push-pull method on systems with large liquid charges) is faster than vapor-only recovery; chilling the recovery cylinder also speeds recovery by lowering its pressure.

When using system-dependent recovery on a small appliance whose compressor does not run, access both the high and low sides and help release refrigerant trapped in the compressor oil (for example, by tapping or warming the compressor).
Solderless piercing (saddle) access valves used for recovering small appliances tend to leak over time and should not be left on the system permanently.

Household refrigerators and freezers using propane (R-290) or isobutane (R-600a) contain exempt substitutes, so those hydrocarbons are not covered by the Section 608 venting prohibition in those listed uses.
facts.note: Local fire codes and manufacturer procedures still apply.

facts.fact: Leak test a high-pressure system by pressurizing with dry nitrogen through a pressure regulator and relief valve; never use oxygen or compressed air, which can explode when mixed with compressor oil under pressure.

Low-pressure chillers (such as R-123) run below atmospheric pressure on the low side, so air and moisture leak in; a purge unit removes these non-condensables, and its frequent operation indicates a leak.

Low-pressure chiller evaporators are protected by a rupture disc typically set at 15 psig, so pressure for leak testing (raised with controlled hot water or heating blankets) should not exceed 10 psig.

When recovering refrigerant from a low-pressure chiller, keep water circulating through the tubes (or drain them) to prevent freezing, because evacuating lowers the refrigerant's saturation temperature below 32 F.

facts.source: Montreal Protocol; Clean Air Act Amendments of 1990
facts.fact: The Montreal Protocol (1987) is the international treaty phasing out ozone-depleting substances; Section 608 of the 1990 Clean Air Act Amendments set the U.S. refrigerant recycling and venting rules.

Chlorine from CFCs and HCFCs damages stratospheric ozone, which shields the earth from ultraviolet (UV-B) radiation; CFCs have the highest ozone depletion potential, HCFCs lower, and HFCs zero ODP but often high global warming potential.

U.S. production of CFCs such as R-12 ended at the end of 1995; manufacture of new equipment designed for R-22 ended January 1, 2010; production and import of R-22 ended January 1, 2020 (only recovered, recycled or reclaimed R-22 remains for servicing); and production of the remaining HCFCs, including R-123, ends January 1, 2030.
facts.reviewed: Misleading by omission. Production and import of R-22 (HCFC-22) ended January 1, 2020, a common exam date. The fact as written suggests R-22 production runs until 2030.

facts.fact: Refrigerant enters the compressor as a low-pressure superheated vapor and leaves as a high-pressure, high-temperature superheated vapor.

In the condenser, refrigerant first gives up superheat (desuperheating), then condenses from vapor to liquid at the saturation temperature, and finally is cooled below saturation (subcooled) before leaving as a high-pressure liquid.
The metering device drops the high-pressure liquid to low pressure; part of the liquid flashes to vapor, so a low-pressure, low-temperature liquid-vapor mixture enters the evaporator.

In the evaporator, the refrigerant absorbs heat from the air and boils at its saturation temperature; once all liquid has boiled, further heat adds superheat before the vapor returns to the compressor through the suction line.

The liquid line carries high-pressure subcooled liquid from the condenser to the metering device, and the suction line carries low-pressure superheated vapor from the evaporator to the compressor (the larger, insulated line on a split system).

Saturation is the condition where liquid and vapor exist together; the pressure-temperature (PT) chart relationship applies only at saturation, such as inside the condenser and evaporator where the refrigerant is changing state.

Subcooling = condenser saturation temperature (from the high-side pressure on a PT chart) minus the actual liquid line temperature. Example: 110 F saturation and a 100 F liquid line gives 10 F of subcooling.
Worked example: if suction pressure corresponds to a 40 F evaporator saturation temperature and the suction line measures 52 F at the evaporator outlet, the superheat is 52 - 40 = 12 F.

At a 40 F saturation temperature, R-22 is at about 68.5 psig while R-410A is at about 118 psig, so R-410A runs at roughly 1.7 times the gauge pressure of R-22 and needs equipment, hoses and gauges rated for it.
Fixed-orifice (piston) and capillary-tube systems are charged by superheat, using the manufacturer's target superheat chart based on indoor wet-bulb and outdoor dry-bulb temperatures.

In a thermostatic expansion valve (TXV), sensing bulb pressure pushes the valve open, while evaporator pressure and spring pressure push it closed; the valve modulates to hold a nearly constant evaporator superheat.

A TXV sensing bulb is strapped to a horizontal section of the suction line near the evaporator outlet, generally at the top (12 o'clock) on lines smaller than 7/8 inch and at about 4 or 8 o'clock on larger lines, and insulated.
facts.note: Follow valve manufacturer guidance.

facts.fact: An electronic expansion valve (EEV) uses a stepper motor driven by an electronic controller that reads temperature and pressure sensors, allowing precise superheat control over a wide range of loads.
Capillary tubes and fixed orifices cannot adjust to load changes, so systems that use them are critically charged and very sensitive to the exact refrigerant amount.
Common compressor types are reciprocating (piston), scroll (most residential AC), rotary, screw (large commercial) and centrifugal (large chillers).

A hermetic compressor seals the motor and compressor in a welded shell; a semi-hermetic compressor is bolted so it can be opened for repair; an open-drive compressor has an external motor connected by a shaft with a shaft seal.
Compression ratio = absolute discharge pressure / absolute suction pressure (add 14.7 to each gauge reading). Example: 250 psig discharge and 70 psig suction gives 264.7 / 84.7 = about 3.1 to 1.
Liquid refrigerant reaching the compressor (floodback or slugging) can damage valves and dilute oil; very low or zero superheat at the compressor is the warning sign.

High superheat with low subcooling usually indicates a refrigerant undercharge; high superheat with high subcooling suggests a liquid line restriction (such as a plugged filter drier) or underfeeding metering device.
Air or other non-condensable gases in a refrigeration system collect in the condenser and cause abnormally high head (discharge) pressure.

A suction-line accumulator protects the compressor from liquid floodback; a receiver stores liquid refrigerant (common with TXV systems); a filter drier in the liquid line removes moisture and debris.
Heat pump reversing valves are energized either in cooling (thermostat terminal O, used by most manufacturers) or in heating (terminal B, used by some brands such as Rheem/Ruud).
During defrost a heat pump switches to cooling mode to send hot gas to the outdoor coil, turns off the outdoor fan, and usually turns on auxiliary heat to temper the cold indoor air.
The balance point is the outdoor temperature at which a heat pump's heating capacity equals the building's heat loss; below it, supplemental heat is needed.
One Btu raises one pound of water one degree F. Latent heat changes state without changing temperature: about 144 Btu/lb to melt ice at 32 F and about 970 Btu/lb to boil water at 212 F.
Useful conversions: 1 kW = 3,412 Btu/h; 1 horsepower = 746 watts = about 2,545 Btu/h; 1 therm = 100,000 Btu.

EER = cooling output in Btu/h divided by power input in watts; COP = output divided by input in the same units (Btu/h / (watts x 3.412)). Example: 36,000 Btu/h at 3,000 W gives EER 12 and COP of about 3.5.

Dry-bulb temperature is ordinary air temperature; wet-bulb temperature is read by a thermometer with a wetted wick and is lowered by evaporation; dew point is the temperature at which moisture begins to condense.
At 100 percent relative humidity (saturated air), dry-bulb, wet-bulb and dew point temperatures are equal; otherwise wet bulb is lower than dry bulb, and dew point is lower still.
Relative humidity compares the moisture in the air to the most it could hold at that temperature; warming air without adding moisture lowers its relative humidity, while its dew point stays the same.
Moisture content (humidity ratio) is often expressed in grains of water per pound of dry air; 7,000 grains equal 1 pound of water.
Enthalpy is the total heat (sensible plus latent) in air, in Btu per pound of dry air; lines of constant wet-bulb temperature are nearly lines of constant enthalpy on the psychrometric chart.
The wet-bulb depression (dry bulb minus wet bulb) measured with a sling psychrometer indicates dryness: the larger the depression, the lower the relative humidity.
Sensible heat ratio (SHR) = sensible load / total load. Example: 18,000 Btu/h sensible out of 24,000 Btu/h total gives SHR = 0.75 (25 percent of the load is latent, or moisture removal).

A cooling coil removes moisture only when its surface is colder than the entering air's dew point; reducing airflow (for example, to about 350 cfm per ton) lowers coil temperature and increases dehumidification, while higher airflow favors sensible cooling.
facts.note: Airflow targets per manufacturer.

facts.source: Q = 0.68 x CFM x delta grains
facts.fact: Latent heat (Btu/h) = 0.68 x CFM x change in moisture (grains per pound). Example: 1,000 CFM with a 20-grain moisture drop removes 0.68 x 1,000 x 20 = 13,600 Btu/h of latent heat.

facts.source: Q = 4.5 x CFM x delta h
facts.fact: Total heat (Btu/h) = 4.5 x CFM x change in enthalpy (Btu/lb), where 4.5 = 0.075 lb/cu ft x 60 min/h. Example: 1,000 CFM with an enthalpy drop of 6 Btu/lb is 4.5 x 1,000 x 6 = 27,000 Btu/h.

facts.source: Q = 1.08 x CFM x delta T
facts.fact: The 1.08 in the sensible heat formula comes from standard air density (0.075 lb/cu ft) x 60 minutes per hour x specific heat of air (0.24 Btu/lb-F).

facts.source: Q = 1.08 x CFM x delta T
facts.fact: Solving for airflow: CFM = sensible Btu/h / (1.08 x delta T). Example: removing 24,000 Btu/h of sensible heat with a 20 F supply-air temperature drop requires 24,000 / (1.08 x 20) = about 1,111 CFM.

facts.source: Q = 1.08 x CFM x delta T
facts.fact: Furnace temperature rise = output Btu/h / (1.08 x CFM). Example: an 80,000 Btu/h input furnace at 80 percent efficiency delivers 64,000 Btu/h; at 1,200 CFM the rise is 64,000 / 1,296 = about 49 F, which should fall within the rating plate's temperature-rise range.
Electric heat output = watts x 3.412 Btu/h. Example: a 10 kW heat strip produces 34,120 Btu/h; at 1,000 CFM the temperature rise is 34,120 / (1.08 x 1,000) = about 31.6 F.
Air conditioning systems are commonly designed for about 400 CFM of airflow per ton (normal range about 350 to 450). Example: a 3.5-ton system needs about 3.5 x 400 = 1,400 CFM.
facts.note: Manufacturer specifications govern.

facts.fact: Duct air velocity (feet per minute) = CFM / duct cross-sectional area in square feet. Example: 800 CFM through a 12 x 8 inch duct (96 sq in = 0.667 sq ft) moves at 800 / 0.667 = about 1,200 fpm.
Round duct area = pi x radius squared. Example: an 8-inch round duct has an area of 3.1416 x (4/12)^2 = 0.349 sq ft, so 400 CFM moves at 400 / 0.349 = about 1,146 fpm.
Fan law 1: airflow varies directly with fan speed. Example: a fan delivering 1,000 CFM at 1,000 RPM delivers 1,200 CFM at 1,200 RPM.

Fan law 2: static pressure varies with the square of fan speed. Example: increasing speed 20 percent (ratio 1.2) raises static pressure by 1.2 squared = 1.44 times, so 0.50 in w.c. becomes 0.72 in w.c.
Fan law 3: fan horsepower varies with the cube of fan speed. Example: increasing speed 20 percent raises horsepower by 1.2 cubed = 1.728 times, so a 1 hp load becomes about 1.73 hp.

Total external static pressure is measured with a manometer as the sum of the supply-side and return-side static pressure magnitudes across the air handler. Example: +0.30 in w.c. supply and -0.20 in w.c. return equals 0.50 in w.c. total.

Velocity pressure (in w.c.) = (velocity in fpm / 4,005) squared, and total pressure = static pressure + velocity pressure. Example: air at 1,000 fpm has a velocity pressure of (1,000/4,005)^2 = about 0.062 in w.c.

In Manual D duct design, friction rate (in w.c. per 100 ft) = available static pressure x 100 / total effective length of the longest run. Example: 0.20 in w.c. available over a 250 ft total effective length gives 0.20 x 100 / 250 = 0.08 in w.c. per 100 ft.

facts.source: Q = U x A x delta T
facts.fact: Conduction heat loss = U x area x temperature difference, where U = 1 / total R-value. Example: 100 sq ft of wall at R-13 (U = 0.077) with a 50 F indoor-outdoor difference loses 0.077 x 100 x 50 = about 385 Btu/h.

Infiltration CFM = air changes per hour x house volume (cu ft) / 60, and its sensible load = 1.08 x CFM x delta T. Example: 0.5 ACH in a 16,000 cu ft house is 133 CFM; at a 50 F difference that is 1.08 x 133 x 50 = about 7,200 Btu/h.
ACCA Manual J residential load calculations use the 99 percent heating design dry-bulb temperature and the 1 percent cooling design dry-bulb temperature for the location.

Manual S generally limits single-speed air conditioners and heat pumps (cooling) to a total capacity of 90 to 115 percent of the calculated total cooling load, with larger allowances for multi-stage and variable-speed equipment.
facts.note: Limits vary by Manual S edition and equipment type; confirm with the current Manual S.

facts.fact: On HVAC equipment nameplates, MCA (minimum circuit ampacity) is used to size the branch-circuit conductors, and MOCP (maximum overcurrent protection) is the largest fuse or breaker allowed; the overcurrent device may not exceed the MOCP.
A disconnecting means must be located within sight of air-conditioning and refrigeration equipment; within sight means visible and not more than 50 ft away.
Compressor nameplates list RLA (rated load amps, the running current at rated conditions) and LRA (locked rotor amps, the high inrush current at startup or when the rotor is stalled).

A replacement run capacitor must match the original microfarad (uF) rating within tolerance and have an equal or higher voltage rating; a dual run capacitor has terminals marked C (common), HERM (compressor) and FAN.

A run capacitor stays in the circuit continuously (as on PSC motors); a start capacitor provides a short burst of starting torque and is removed from the circuit by a potential (start) relay or similar device once the motor is up to speed.

PSC (permanent split capacitor) blower motors run at fixed tapped speeds, while ECM (electronically commutated) motors use an integrated electronic control for variable speed and much higher efficiency.
A contactor's 24-volt coil is energized by the thermostat's Y (cooling) circuit, closing contacts that send line voltage to the compressor and condenser fan motor.

Standard thermostat terminals: R = 24 V hot from the transformer, C = common, W = heat, Y = cooling/compressor, G = indoor fan; most residential control transformers supply 24 VAC (often rated 40 VA).
A three-phase motor's rotation is reversed by swapping any two of the three supply leads; a three-phase scroll compressor running backward is noisy and does not pump.

Since January 1, 2023, residential central AC and heat pump efficiency is rated in SEER2, EER2 and HSPF2 under DOE's M1 test procedure, which uses higher external static pressure to better represent real duct systems, so SEER2 numbers are lower than old SEER numbers for the same unit.
In DOE's North region, the 2023 minimum for split-system central air conditioners is 13.4 SEER2 (equivalent to the old 14 SEER).

In DOE's Southeast and Southwest regions (Tennessee is in the Southeast), split-system central air conditioners must be at least 14.3 SEER2 under 45,000 Btu/h and 13.8 SEER2 at 45,000 Btu/h and above.

DOE's Southwest region (Arizona, California, Nevada, New Mexico) adds EER2 minimums for split air conditioners: 11.7 EER2 under 45,000 Btu/h and 11.2 EER2 at 45,000 Btu/h and above (9.8 EER2 if SEER2 is 15.2 or higher).
Nationwide 2023 minimums for heat pumps are 14.3 SEER2 and 7.5 HSPF2 for split systems, and 13.4 SEER2 and 6.7 HSPF2 for single-package units; packaged air conditioners need 13.4 SEER2.

SEER/SEER2 is a seasonal cooling efficiency (seasonal Btu removed / watt-hours used), while EER/EER2 is measured at a single hot condition (95 F outdoor); HSPF/HSPF2 is seasonal heating Btu per watt-hour for heat pumps.

AFUE (annual fuel utilization efficiency) is the percentage of a furnace's or boiler's yearly fuel energy delivered as useful heat; an 80 percent AFUE furnace is typically non-condensing (Category I), while 90 percent and above is condensing (Category IV).
The current federal minimum for non-weatherized residential gas furnaces is 80 percent AFUE.

DOE's December 2023 rule sets a 95 percent AFUE minimum for non-weatherized and mobile home gas furnaces made on or after December 18, 2028; as of May 2026 DOE was taking comment on a petition to delay compliance to at least January 1, 2030.
facts.note: Status in flux; confirm the current compliance date before relying on it.

facts.source: Ala. Code 34-8-1 (as amended by Act 2024-277); Alabama Licensing Board for General Contractors
facts.fact: Commercial general contractors in Alabama are licensed by the Alabama Licensing Board for General Contractors. Since October 1, 2024 (Act 2024-277), a license is required when the cost of the undertaking, including labor and materials, is $100,000 or more; the old threshold was $50,000. Subcontractors performing contracts of $100,000 or more must also be licensed.
facts.note: Confirmed on the board's law page and its Act 2024-277 notice: https://genconbd.alabama.gov/law/ and https://genconbd.alabama.gov/14104/changes-to-the-alabama-licensing-board-for-general-contractors-section-of-the-code-of-alabama/ ; statute text at https://law.justia.com/codes/alabama/title-34/chapter-8/section-34-8-1/

facts.source: Ala. Code 34-8-1(b); Alabama Licensing Board for General Contractors
facts.fact: In Alabama, anyone who builds, supervises, repairs or renovates a swimming pool for compensation must hold a general contractor license from the Alabama Licensing Board for General Contractors when the work is $5,000 or more, a much lower threshold than the $100,000 rule for other commercial work.
facts.note: Board law page: https://genconbd.alabama.gov/law/ ('Swimming Pool construction of $5,000 or more'); older code text on Justia says 'exceeding $5,000': https://law.justia.com/codes/alabama/title-34/chapter-8/section-34-8-1/
facts.reviewed: The board's law page (reflecting the 2024 amendments) states the pool trigger as '$5,000 or more'; the fact said 'over $5,000'. A $5,000 pool job would be wrongly treated as exempt. Use the stricter board wording.

facts.source: Ala. Code 34-14A-2; Alabama Home Builders Licensure Board
facts.fact: Residential construction in Alabama is licensed separately by the Home Builders Licensure Board. A residential home builder license is required when the cost of the undertaking exceeds $10,000, and residential roofers must be licensed when the roofing job exceeds $2,500.
facts.note: Statute text: https://law.justia.com/codes/alabama/title-34/chapter-14a/section-34-14a-2/

facts.source: Alabama Licensing Board for General Contractors, Testing page; PSI Candidate Information Bulletin, Alabama General Contractors (updated 1/23/26)
facts.fact: Alabama general contractor exams are given by PSI. Applicants (since January 22, 2008) must pass a trade exam for their classification plus the Business and Law exam. The Business and Law exam is 50 questions, 120 minutes, open book, and needs 70% to pass; the one reference is the NASCLA Contractor's Guide to Business, Law and Project Management, Alabama General, 3rd edition.
facts.note: https://genconbd.alabama.gov/licensees/testing/ and PSI bulletin https://test-takers.psiexams.com/api/content/bulletin/76 . References may be highlighted/tabbed with permanent tabs only; no loose papers.

facts.source: PSI Candidate Information Bulletin, Alabama General Contractors (updated 1/23/26)
facts.fact: Alabama offers the NASCLA-accredited Commercial General Building Contractor exam (115 questions, 330 minutes, 81 correct to pass) as a trade exam option. The Building Contractor Under Four Stories exam is 90 questions in 230 minutes with 70% (63 correct) needed to pass.
facts.note: PSI bulletin: https://test-takers.psiexams.com/api/content/bulletin/76

facts.source: Alabama Licensing Board for General Contractors, Reciprocity and How to Apply pages
facts.fact: Alabama's general contractor board has reciprocity with Arkansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, North Carolina and Tennessee. A licensee in good standing in a comparable classification in one of those states (qualified by the same person) may have the trade exam waived on written certification from that state, but the Business and Law exam is never waived, and the application must be on file 30 days before a reciprocal license issues.
facts.note: https://genconbd.alabama.gov/licensees/reciprocity/ and https://genconbd.alabama.gov/licensees/apply/ . Board page does not mention NASCLA reciprocity beyond offering the NASCLA exam.
facts.reviewed: Board reciprocity page does not state a 1-year licensure minimum; it requires a license in good standing in a comparable classification held by the same qualifier. Removed the unsupported '(licensed 1 year)'.

facts.source: Alabama Licensing Board for General Contractors, How to Apply page
facts.fact: Prime contractor applications to the Alabama general contractor board must be on file 30 days before a quarterly board meeting. Subcontractor applicants must submit three references from general contractors, architects, engineers or awarding authorities, and a subcontractor may bid to a general contractor but cannot start work until licensed.
facts.note: https://genconbd.alabama.gov/licensees/apply/ . Financial statement and bid-limit rules are in Ala. Admin. Code 230-X-1-.02 and -.19 but were not readable in this session.

facts.source: Alabama Licensing Board for General Contractors, Renewal Information page
facts.fact: Alabama general contractor license renewals are staggered by month according to the first letter of the company name and are filed online. If a license is not renewed within one year after expiration, the contractor must reapply and retake the trade and Business and Law exams.
facts.note: https://genconbd.alabama.gov/licensees/renewal-information/ . The page does not mention continuing education for general contractors.

facts.fact: Electrical work in Alabama is licensed statewide by the Alabama Electrical Contractors Board, which issues electrical contractor licenses and journeyman electrician licenses. The board has announced that 2027 is a continuing education year in which electrical contractors must complete 14 hours of CE; check the board for the journeyman requirement and which years are CE years.
facts.note: https://aecb.alabama.gov/ (home page notice). Journeyman CE hours were not stated on the page.
facts.reviewed: Board notice says '2027 is a CE year' and electrical contractors need 14 hours; CE is tied to designated CE years rather than every renewal. Reworded so students do not assume 14 hours every year.

facts.source: Ala. Code 34-37-1; Alabama Plumbers and Gas Fitters Examining Board
facts.fact: The Alabama Plumbers and Gas Fitters Examining Board certifies master plumbers, journeyman plumbers, master gas fitters, journeyman gas fitters and registered apprentices, all on annual certificates. A plumbing or gas business must register a certified master as its principal, and medical gas piping work needs an added medical gas certificate.
facts.note: Statute: https://law.justia.com/codes/alabama/title-34/chapter-37/section-34-37-1/ . Board site https://pgfb.alabama.gov/ says CE for 2027 renewals must be done before November 1, 2026 (renewal window Oct 1 to Dec 31).

facts.source: Ala. Code 34-31-18 et seq.; Alabama Board of Heating, Air Conditioning and Refrigeration Contractors
facts.fact: HVAC and refrigeration contractors in Alabama are certified by testing through the State Board of Heating, Air Conditioning and Refrigeration Contractors.
facts.note: Board name confirmed in Ala. Code 34-31-18 (https://law.justia.com/codes/alabama/title-34/chapter-31/section-34-31-18/), but the board website blocked fetching, so certification classes, exam provider and CE were not confirmed.

facts.fact: In Alabama, a supplier or subcontractor without a direct contract with the owner gets a lien for the full price only if it notifies the owner in writing before furnishing the material (and the owner does not object in writing before it is used). Without that notice, the lien is limited to the unpaid balance the owner still owes the contractor.
facts.note: https://law.justia.com/codes/alabama/title-35/chapter-11/article-5/division-8/section-35-11-210/

facts.fact: Alabama lien statements must be filed with the probate judge within 6 months after the last work or materials for an original contractor, within 30 days for journeymen and day laborers, and within 4 months for everyone else (subs and suppliers). A suit to enforce the lien must be filed within 6 months after the entire debt matures.
facts.note: https://law.justia.com/codes/alabama/title-35/chapter-11/article-5/division-8/section-35-11-215/ and https://law.justia.com/codes/alabama/title-35/chapter-11/article-5/division-8/section-35-11-221/

facts.fact: Arizona contractors (general and trade) are licensed by the Arizona Registrar of Contractors (ROC). The 'handyman' exemption covers only jobs with a total price, including labor and materials, under $1,000 that do not need a building permit, and the person may not advertise without stating 'not a licensed contractor'.
facts.note: Statute: https://www.azleg.gov/ars/32/01121.htm

facts.source: Arizona Registrar of Contractors, Applying for a License
facts.fact: An Arizona ROC license needs a qualifying party who is regularly employed by the business, at least 18, and meets the classification's minimum years of experience. Applicants and qualifying parties must submit a background check (valid 90 days) and proof of a license bond.
facts.note: https://azroc.gov/applying-for-a-license . Experience years per classification are in the ROC License Classification Requirements form (not read in this session).

facts.source: Arizona Registrar of Contractors, Applying for a License; PSI AZ ROC Candidate Information Bulletin (2/18/2026)
facts.fact: Arizona applicants take the Statutes and Rules Exam (SRE), an online ROC training course plus exam delivered only through Gmetrix, which the ROC says cannot be waived, and a trade exam through PSI (online or at a test center). The qualifying party must pass the required exams with at least 70%.
facts.note: https://azroc.gov/applying-for-a-license and PSI bulletin https://test-takers.psiexams.com/api/content/bulletin/5617 . Question counts/time are in each trade's content outline, not the main bulletin.
facts.reviewed: Internal contradiction: the ROC page says the SRE 'cannot be waived' and that the qualifying party must complete it, but the fact also said it is required only for those not listed as a qualifying party in the last five years. The five-year rule on the ROC page applies to waiving the trade exam, not the SRE. Removed the unsupported SRE exemption.

facts.source: Arizona Registrar of Contractors, Applying for a License; Ariz. Admin. Code R4-9-106(E)
facts.fact: Arizona B-1 and B-2 general commercial applicants may take the NASCLA Commercial General Building exam in place of the ROC trade exam, and CR-11, C-11 and R-11 electrical applicants may take the NASCLA electrical exam. The trade exam (not the SRE) can be waived if the qualifying party qualified a license in good standing in the same or comparable classification within the past five years.
facts.note: https://azroc.gov/applying-for-a-license

facts.fact: Arizona license bonds depend on license type and estimated annual volume. Under A.R.S. 32-1152 the range is $5,000 to $15,000 for a residential general (B) license and $1,000 to $7,500 for residential specialty; commercial general bonds run from $5,000 (under $150,000 volume) up to $50,000 to $100,000 ($10 million or more). Residential contractors must also join the Residential Contractors' Recovery Fund or post an extra $200,000 bond.
facts.note: Statute: https://www.azleg.gov/ars/32/01152.htm . Exact amounts within each range are set by ROC rule.

facts.fact: In Arizona, a contractor cannot sue to collect payment for work that requires a license unless it alleges and proves it was properly licensed both when the contract was made and when the claim arose.
facts.note: https://www.azleg.gov/ars/32/01153.htm

facts.source: Arizona Registrar of Contractors license classifications
facts.fact: Arizona licenses electrical (e.g., R-11, C-11, CR-11), plumbing (R-37, C-37, CR-37) and HVAC (R-39, C-39, CR-39) work as ROC contractor classifications with residential (R), commercial (C) and dual (CR) versions. Arizona does not issue a statewide journeyman or master electrician or plumber license; individual worker certification, if any, is local.
facts.note: Classification codes R-11/C-11/CR-11 are confirmed on https://azroc.gov/applying-for-a-license; the plumbing/HVAC codes and the absence of state journeyman licensing come from general knowledge and were not confirmed on an official page this session.

facts.fact: Arizona requires a preliminary twenty-day notice as a condition of any lien: it must be served on the owner, original contractor, construction lender and the party the claimant contracted with no later than 20 days after the claimant first furnishes labor or materials. A late notice covers only work furnished within 20 days before it was served and afterward; wage laborers are exempt.
facts.note: https://www.azleg.gov/ars/33/00992-01.htm

facts.fact: An Arizona notice and claim of lien must be recorded within 120 days after completion of the improvement, or within 60 days after a notice of completion is recorded. The lien lapses 6 months after recording unless a foreclosure suit is filed and a notice of pendency of action is recorded within that time.
facts.note: https://www.azleg.gov/ars/33/00993.htm and https://www.azleg.gov/ars/33/00998.htm

facts.fact: In Arizona, a person who is required to be licensed as a contractor but does not hold a valid license has no mechanics' lien rights.
facts.note: https://www.azleg.gov/ars/33/00981.htm

facts.fact: An Arizona contractor license is suspended by law the business day after its renewal date unless a renewal with a valid bond and fee was received or mailed by that date. A suspended license may be renewed within one year (with an added fee); after one year a new application is required. Arizona ROC licenses renew every two years and there is no continuing education requirement.
facts.note: Suspension and one-year reactivation rules confirmed at https://www.azleg.gov/ars/32/01125.htm ; the two-year renewal cycle and no-CE statement were not confirmed on an official page this session.

facts.source: Ark. Code 17-25-101; Arkansas Contractors Licensing Board (Dept. of Labor and Licensing)
facts.fact: The Arkansas Contractors Licensing Board requires a commercial contractor license when the cost of work, including labor and materials, is $50,000 or more. Any project that is not a single-family residence counts as commercial, and a business and law exam is required.
facts.note: Statute: https://law.justia.com/codes/arkansas/title-17/subtitle-2/chapter-25/subchapter-1/section-17-25-101/ ; board page: https://labor.arkansas.gov/licensing/arkansas-contractors-licensing-board/apply-for-contractors-license-registration/

facts.source: Arkansas Contractors Licensing Board, Apply for License page
facts.fact: In Arkansas, a subcontractor working under a properly licensed prime contractor on a commercial job can use a subcontractor registration certificate instead of a full license. If the prime contractor lacks the proper commercial license, the subcontractor needs a commercial license, and a contract directly with the owner is prime contracting.
facts.note: https://labor.arkansas.gov/licensing/arkansas-contractors-licensing-board/apply-for-contractors-license-registration/

facts.source: Ark. Code 17-25-502, -513; Residential Building Contractors Committee law (rev. July 2025)
facts.fact: Residential work in Arkansas (single-family = 1 to 4 units) is licensed by the Residential Building Contractors Committee of the Contractors Licensing Board, which issues residential builder, remodeler and specialty (home improvement) licenses. Projects of $2,000 or less are exempt, but splitting a job into contracts under $2,000 does not qualify.
facts.note: https://labor.arkansas.gov/wp-content/uploads/Residential-Law-revised-July-2025.pdf ; the board page says the home improvement license applies to specialty work over $2,000 on a single-family residence.

facts.source: PSI Candidate Information Bulletin, Arkansas Contractors Licensing Board (updated 6/3/2022)
facts.fact: Every Arkansas contractor classification must pass the Arkansas Contractor Business and Law exam plus any trade exam. The Business and Law exam is 50 questions, 120 minutes, open book, and needs 35 correct (70%); the only allowed reference is the NASCLA Contractor's Guide to Business, Law and Project Management, Arkansas edition (8th edition in the 2022 bulletin).
facts.note: PSI bulletin: https://test-takers.psiexams.com/api/content/bulletin/6936 . Bulletin is dated 2022; confirm the current required edition before testing. An older Prometric bulletin (2019) used the 6th edition.

facts.source: Ark. Code 17-25-304; ACLB Bond in Lieu of Financial Statement form
facts.fact: Arkansas commercial applicants must submit a financial statement reviewed by a CPA or licensed public accountant (a compiled statement is allowed for a single project under $1,500,000). Instead, they may post a surety bond of 10 times the required net worth for the classification, e.g., $500,000 for Building or Heavy, $200,000 for Light Building, Mechanical or Electrical, and $50,000 for Specialty.
facts.note: https://law.justia.com/codes/arkansas/title-17/subtitle-2/chapter-25/subchapter-3/section-17-25-304/ and https://www.labor.arkansas.gov/wp-content/uploads/Commercial-Bond-in-Lieu-of-Financial_0721.pdf (form dated 07/21).

facts.fact: Arkansas residential builders and unlimited remodelers/specialty contractors must file a sworn compiled financial statement showing positive net worth for work of $50,000 or more, and must show workers' compensation coverage before a license is issued or renewed. A lapse in workers' comp coverage requires the committee to revoke the license.
facts.note: https://labor.arkansas.gov/wp-content/uploads/Residential-Law-revised-July-2025.pdf

facts.fact: An Arkansas residential contractor who works without the required license cannot sue to enforce the contract or recover under quantum meruit.
facts.note: https://labor.arkansas.gov/wp-content/uploads/Residential-Law-revised-July-2025.pdf

facts.source: Arkansas Dept. of Labor and Licensing, Electrical Inspection and Licensing
facts.fact: The Arkansas Board of Electrical Examiners (Dept. of Labor and Licensing) licenses master, journeyman, residential master and residential journeyman electricians, plus air conditioning and industrial maintenance electricians, and registers apprentices.
facts.note: https://labor.arkansas.gov/labor/code-enforcement/electrical-inspection-and-licensing/

facts.source: Arkansas Dept. of Labor and Licensing, HVAC/R
facts.fact: Arkansas HVAC/R licenses (Classes A, B, D and E among others) are issued through the Department of Labor and Licensing and the State HVAC/R Board; applicants must be pre-approved by the board to sit for the exam. The HVAC/R board has no reciprocal licensing agreements with other states.
facts.note: https://labor.arkansas.gov/labor/code-enforcement/hvac-r/ . The page did not describe the scope of each class.

facts.source: Arkansas Department of Health, Plumbing and Natural Gas Section
facts.fact: Plumbers in Arkansas are licensed by the Arkansas Department of Health (Plumbing and Natural Gas Section), not the Contractors Licensing Board, with master and journeyman plumber licenses.
facts.note: The Department of Health page could not be fetched this session; based on general knowledge and secondary sites.

facts.fact: On Arkansas residential jobs (4 or fewer units), the contractor must give the owner the statutory lien notice before work begins, or neither the contractor nor anyone else can claim a lien (unless a payment and performance bond is provided). On commercial jobs, subs, suppliers and laborers must send the owner and contractor a notice of nonpayment within 75 days after furnishing labor or materials to keep lien rights.
facts.note: https://law.justia.com/codes/arkansas/title-18/subtitle-4/chapter-44/subchapter-1/section-18-44-115/

facts.fact: An Arkansas lien claimant must give the owner 10 days' notice before filing, then file the lien with the circuit clerk within 120 days after the last materials or labor were furnished. A suit to enforce the lien must be commenced within 15 months after filing.
facts.note: https://law.justia.com/codes/arkansas/title-18/subtitle-4/chapter-44/subchapter-1/section-18-44-117/ ; .../section-18-44-114/ ; .../section-18-44-119/

facts.fact: Arkansas residential licenses expire one year after issuance unless the committee offers a two- or three-year renewal. A license may be renewed up to two years after expiration (with a late fee within 30 days); after that a new application is needed.
facts.note: https://labor.arkansas.gov/wp-content/uploads/Residential-Law-revised-July-2025.pdf

facts.source: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code 7048 (as amended by AB 1170, eff. Jan. 1, 2026); Contractors State License Board
facts.fact: California contractors are licensed by the Contractors State License Board (CSLB). The minor work exemption covers only small, non-substantial jobs with a total price (labor, materials and everything else) under $1,000 that need no building permit; it does not apply if the work is part of a larger job, is split up to evade the law, or the person advertises as a contractor or hires others to help.
facts.note: Statute text (2025 code reflecting AB 1170, effective 1/1/2026): https://law.justia.com/codes/california/code-bpc/division-3/chapter-9/article-3/section-7048/ . The limit was $500 for many years; older study materials still say $500.

facts.fact: A California license applicant (or qualifier) needs at least 4 years of experience at the journeyman, foreman, supervising employee or contractor level in the classification, gained within the 10 years before applying. Accredited schooling or an approved apprenticeship can count for up to 3 of the 4 years.
facts.note: Regulation text: https://www.law.cornell.edu/regulations/california/16-CCR-825

facts.source: CSLB Apply for a License and Contractor License pages; Bus. & Prof. Code 7065
facts.fact: California applicants must pass two CSLB exams, Law and Business and a trade exam (no trade exam for the C-61 Limited Specialty class), and then complete the Asbestos Open Book Exam. No exam is needed if the person served as a qualifier in good standing for the same classification, or passed both exams, within the past five years.
facts.note: https://www.cslb.ca.gov/Contractors/Applicants and https://www.cslb.ca.gov/Contractors/Applicants/Contractors_License/ . Question counts and time limits were not stated on the pages fetched.

facts.source: CSLB Bond Requirements page; Bus. & Prof. Code 7071.6
facts.fact: Since January 1, 2023, every active California contractor license must carry a $25,000 contractor's bond, and a responsible managing employee qualifier must post a separate $25,000 Bond of Qualifying Individual. A disciplinary bond, when ordered, is at least $25,000 and up to 10 times the contractor's bond.
facts.note: https://cslb.ca.gov/contractors/maintain_license/bond_information/bond_requirements.aspx

facts.fact: A California contractor who needed a license cannot sue to collect payment unless it was duly licensed at all times during the work, and an owner who hired an unlicensed contractor can sue to recover all compensation already paid (disgorgement).
facts.note: Statute text via FindLaw: https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/business-and-professions-code/bpc-sect-7031/

facts.fact: California home improvement contracts over $500 must follow B&P 7159: the down payment may not exceed $1,000 or 10% of the contract price, whichever is less, and the buyer may cancel within 3 business days after receiving the signed contract (5 days for senior citizen buyers).
facts.note: Statute text via FindLaw: https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/business-and-professions-code/bpc-sect-7159/

facts.source: CSLB license classifications; Cal. Labor Code 3099-3099.4 (DIR electrician certification)
facts.fact: California licenses electrical, plumbing and HVAC businesses as CSLB specialty contractors (C-10 Electrical, C-36 Plumbing, C-20 Warm-Air HVAC). Workers doing electrical work for a C-10 contractor must also hold a state electrician certification from the Department of Industrial Relations (e.g., General Electrician), or be registered apprentices. There is no statewide journeyman plumber or HVAC license.
facts.note: Classification codes and the DIR certification rule are from general knowledge; the CSLB classification page and DIR pages failed to load this session, so details (and hour requirements) were not confirmed.

facts.source: Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code 7140; CSLB Reciprocity page
facts.fact: California contractor licenses run for two years from the last day of the month issued, and a timely renewal continues the license another two years. CSLB has reciprocity programs with Arizona, Louisiana and Nevada.
facts.note: https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/business-and-professions-code/bpc-sect-7140/ and https://www.cslb.ca.gov/Contractors/Applicants/Reciprocity/ . The reciprocity page did not state which exam is waived (commonly the trade exam, with Law and Business still required).

facts.fact: In California, a preliminary notice must be given no later than 20 days after the claimant first furnishes work. A late notice still works, but lien, stop payment notice and payment bond rights then cover only work performed within 20 days before the notice was served and after.
facts.note: Statute text via FindLaw: https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/civil-code/civ-sect-8204/

facts.fact: A California direct contractor must record its lien after finishing its contract and before the earlier of 90 days after completion of the project or 60 days after the owner records a notice of completion or cessation. Other claimants (subs, suppliers) have the earlier of 90 days after completion or 30 days after a notice of completion or cessation. A suit to enforce the lien must be filed within 90 days after recording.
facts.note: Statute text via FindLaw: https://codes.findlaw.com/ca/civil-code/civ-sect-8412/ , /civ-sect-8414/ , /civ-sect-8460/

facts.source: Colorado Division of Professions and Occupations (DORA); local building departments
facts.fact: Colorado has no statewide general contractor license. General, building and specialty contractors are licensed or registered by cities and counties (for example Denver, Colorado Springs/Pikes Peak Regional Building Department), often with ICC exams, while the state (DORA) licenses only electricians and plumbers among the construction trades.
facts.note: Consistent across many secondary sources and with DORA's program list, but no official state page saying 'no state GC license' was confirmed this session.

facts.fact: The Colorado State Electrical Board licenses Master Electricians, Journeyman Electricians and Residential Wiremen. A journeyman needs at least 4 years of apprenticeship or practical experience (at least 2 years commercial/industrial) plus 288 hours of training in safety and the NEC; a residential wireman needs 2 years of training or experience in 1- to 4-family dwellings.
facts.note: Board page https://dpo.colorado.gov/Electrical ; statute text via FindLaw https://codes.findlaw.com/co/title-12-professions-and-occupations/co-rev-st-sect-12-115-110/

facts.fact: A Colorado Master Electrician applicant generally needs at least one year of experience planning, laying out and supervising electrical work beyond the journeyman requirements (other routes: an engineering graduate with one year of practical construction experience, or a trade school graduate with four years of practical experience). The board or its designee conducts the exam.
facts.note: Statute text via FindLaw: https://codes.findlaw.com/co/title-12-professions-and-occupations/co-rev-st-sect-12-115-110/

facts.fact: Colorado Residential Wiremen, Journeyman and Master Electricians must complete 24 hours of continuing education during each 3-year license period, from board-attested providers. Licenses run on 3-year periods ending September 30 (the most recent period ended September 30, 2026, with late renewal allowed through November 30, 2026); check the board for the current deadline.
facts.note: https://dpo.colorado.gov/Electrical . Those first licensed by exam in the current period need no CE until after their first renewal.
facts.reviewed: Time-sensitive wording goes stale: as of October 2026 the September 30, 2026 expiration has already passed and the November 30, 2026 renewal window closes within weeks. Rewritten so it stays true after this cycle.

facts.fact: The Colorado State Plumbing Board licenses Residential Plumbers, Journeyworker Plumbers ('journeyman' renamed effective July 1, 2025) and Master Plumbers. By statute the board may require up to 3,400 hours of practical experience for residential, 6,800 hours for journeyworker and 8,500 hours for master; a board-approved plumbing program counts as one year of experience.
facts.note: https://dpo.colorado.gov/Plumbing ; statute via FindLaw https://codes.findlaw.com/co/title-12-professions-and-occupations/co-rev-st-sect-12-155-110/ (statute gives maximums; the board rule sets the actual minimums).

facts.fact: Colorado plumbing licenses run for a two-year period. Active Residential, Journeyworker and Master Plumbers must complete at least 8 hours of continuing education each licensure year (March 1 through February 28) from board-attested providers.
facts.note: https://dpo.colorado.gov/Plumbing

facts.fact: Colorado does not issue a state HVAC or mechanical license; mechanical contractors are licensed by local jurisdictions where required.
